Houdini 22.0.368's viewport OCIO display shows linear values below about 0.004 as black and lowers values up to about 0.05, although OCIO's CPU processor and OCIO 2.5's GPU shader for the same view are the exact sRGB curve. Reproduce with Launch-Houdini.ps1 -TestKind parity -InputUsd <stage> and HDUE_TEST_CAMERA: it writes the delegate's frame (viewport.pfm) and flipbooks with the viewport's OCIO on and off.

items.title: AOVs
items.text:
src/hydra/aov_table.h is the AOV table; scripts/build_render_settings_hda.py reads it for the Houdini assets. Requests go through include/hdue/bridge.h (HDUE_AOV_*), with their own UE view state and frame slot, so the beauty's Lumen or Path Tracer history is unaffected.

  • Buffer AOVs: one raster render with Movie Render Queue's buffer visualization pipes (FinalPostProcessSettings.BufferVisualizationPipes, as MoviePipelineDeferredPasses), Lumen, anti-aliasing and post effects off. With velocity, the pass first renders the previous frame (unpublished) so UE's velocity buffer holds the motion since then.
  • Path Tracer albedo and normal: read back from the converged beauty (PathTracingBufferTexture), used when the AOV request shows the same view; a motion-blurred beauty falls back to the raster buffers.
  • Lighting components: the Path Tracer's PathTracingInclude* settings; realtime uses the Diffuse, Specular and Direct Lighting show flags and turns Lumen GI or reflections off. The tonemapper and eye adaptation show flags are off for every AOV.
  • ID passes: generated materials switch to emitting the prim ID from custom primitive data 5 (IdSwitch.cpp), keeping their cutout opacity; meshes with cooked native materials draw M_HdUEId, which ignores cutout opacity. unreal:cvar:r:HdUE:IdSwap = 1 swaps every mesh.
  • Cryptomatte: 16 primId passes on a 4 x 4 sub-pixel grid; ids are MurmurHash3_32 of the prim or material path (src/hydra/cryptomatte.h). The metadata reaches husk through the render stats and husk.metadata in UsdRenderers.json.

items.title: Alpha
items.text: r.PostProcessing.PropagateAlpha=True is set in DefaultEngine.ini (before TSR caches its alpha permutation). UE keeps 1 - coverage in scene colour alpha; the readback (Bridge.cpp, SharedFrame.usf) outputs coverage. The realtime HDRI background (Environment.usf) writes alpha 1 into scene colour, which is coverage 0.

items.title: Rendering internals
items.text: Implementation notes behind the user pages on render settings, denoising, motion blur, debug views and engine quality.

items.title: Render settings
items.text: unreal:* attributes on the UsdRenderSettings prim reach the delegate as render settings with the unreal: prefix stripped. String settings accept string or token (Houdini's menus author tokens); numbers accept any numeric type. In Houdini's viewport, houdini:interactive (tumbling, scrubbing, playing) caps Path Tracer samples at 8 (HdUEState::samples in src/hydra/delegate.h) and skips the ID AOV passes; a change of houdini:interactive is a new request.

items.title: Offline profile
items.text: Bridge.cpp applies Movie Render Queue's Game Overrides when the host is not interactive (husk), before any session, so authored unreal:cvar:* values override them: Cinematic scalability keeping the resolution quality, r.Streaming.FullyLoadUsedTextures 1 (with FramesForFullUpdate 0 and SyncStatesWhenBlocking 1), r.D3D12.GPUTimeout 0, Lumen surface cache updates every frame (r.LumenScene.Radiosity.UpdateFactor 2, DirectLighting.UpdateFactor 2, SurfaceCache.CardCapturesPerFrame 100000, CardCaptureFactor 4, as Movie Render Graph's layer warm-ups raise them, DeferredLayerWarmUpHelpers.cpp), and the heterogeneous volume settings UE's docs recommend for cinematic renders (shading rate 1, 512 MB). Each change is logged with UE's value before it; scripts/Test-RenderSettings.ps1 compares the generated defaults with those values.

items.title: Denoiser
items.text:
NNEDenoiser registers its denoiser from a view extension. The backend runs UE's active view extensions on every view family, as Movie Render Queue does (MoviePipelineImagePassBase.cpp).

A host that exits with UE running (husk) ends in the backend's DllMain, before the backend's static destructors. UE's denoiser registry would otherwise release NNEDenoiser's ONNX Runtime session into DirectML and the GPU driver after the exit had ended UE's threads (a fail-fast, 0xC0000409). onnxruntime.dll is loaded before the backend (src/client/backend.cpp) so that it detaches after it; loaded later, it detached first and husk never exited.

UE does not stage the files the OptiX plugin loads from its Source folder (OptiXDenoiseBase.dll and its CUDA kernels, OptiXDenoiserFunctionList.ptx); Stage-Runtime.ps1 copies them. Without the kernels the image stayed black. In UE 5.8.4 the plugin's default 256 x 256 tiles fail in the prebuilt library (OPTIX_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE) and leave a garbled 384-pixel strip, so the runtime sets r.OptixDenoise.TileWidth and TileHeight to 0.

Measurements on the glossy Cornell box at 1920 x 1080 and 32 samples (noise as mean absolute Laplacian): none 0.00303, NNEDenoiser 0.00015, OptiX 0.00009; mean brightness 0.0291, 0.0290, 0.0291.

items.title: Motion blur
items.text: The delegate renders unreal:motionSamples sub-frames when the camera shutter is open, disableMotionBlur and instantaneousShutter are off, and the camera or a mesh moves (delegate.cpp). Lumen keeps its history between sub-frames, so the warmup and the Path Tracer samples are divided between them. Deforming meshes are uploaded again for each sub-frame. Time-sampled PointInstancer placements without velocities and angularVelocities become a velocity and an angular velocity per instance, interpolated between the first and last sample around the frame, as UsdGeomPointInstancer::ComputeInstanceTransformsAtTime does. Velocities are converted with houdini:fps, else framesPerSecond (24) (HdUEFramesPerSecond in prims.cpp). In Realtime, UE's MotionBlurAmount is the shutter interval in frames divided by the motion samples, unless authored.

items.title: Debug views
items.text:
unreal:debugView sets the view mode the way UE's game viewport sets it: view mode show flags, the view's visualization name and material overrides. Buffer views are linear; the others are drawn through UE's tonemapper, as with unreal:tonemapper.

Not offered in the cooked runtime: Wireframe (UE composites it in the editor-primitives pass, compiled into editor builds only), Shader Complexity, Quad Overdraw, LOD coloration and the other material debug modes (their shaders are cooked only with r.ForceDebugViewModes=1, for every material), and the Lightmap modes. Cooked runtimes leave UE's buffer visualization data uninitialized, so hdUE blends the buffer materials (/Engine/BufferVisualization, cooked through DirectoriesToAlwaysCook) as post-process materials itself.

items.title: DLSS
items.text: The DLSS plugin enables itself only for game and editor viewports, so hdUE adds its view extension to each realtime frame, as the plugin's Movie Render Queue support does. Ray Reconstruction is switched with the plugin's EnableDLSSRR, which turns off the denoisers it replaces (r.Shadow.Denoiser, Lumen reflections' temporal and screen-space reconstruction and bilateral filter) and restores them. With DLSS on, the viewport's moving frames size their buffers to their own percentage, as UE's dynamic resolution keeps to the upscaler's range. Launch-Houdini.ps1 -TestKind dlss -InputUsd samples\smoke.usda -RuntimeConfig <a DLSS runtime> checks it in Houdini's viewport.

items.title: Substrate Builder internals
items.text: The user guide is Substrate Builder; this page records how the Builder is implemented and validated. Status: experimental implementation. Houdini VOP authoring, USD graph serialization, editor-side material generation, and Lumen/Path Tracer rendering are implemented. The owned Solaris regression passes eight interactive cases. This document describes the current interfaces and their limits; a working node connection alone does not qualify every possible shader graph.

items.title: Purpose and scope
items.text:
The hdUE Substrate Material Builder lets artists compose UE Substrate materials in a Houdini VOP network. A prepared MaterialX surface can become an input to a larger graph. Slabs, coverage weights, and layer operators are authored explicitly. Water coating is an example network built from these nodes.

The initial implementation targets generic USD meshes in Solaris. Prepared graphs also render through the standalone Hydra host. usdview binds a prepared Builder library with --hdue-substrate-library, after its MaterialX library.

The renderer continues to use one UE instance in the host process. Shader graphs are compiled and cooked by a separate editor process. Solaris can prepare node/wiring edits in the background and install completed material variants without restarting Houdini or UE. Numeric/color inputs are generated as runtime parameters, so ordinary value edits and float masks do not recompile the graph.

items.title: System structure
items.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Houdini["fal:fa-house Houdini"]
        V("fal:fa-workflow Houdini VOP network")
        A("fal:fa-library Material Library LOP<br/>hdUE shader translator")
        U("fal:fa-file-code USD Material and Shader graph")
    end
    subgraph Delegate["fal:fa-package hdUE"]
        P("fal:fa-list-checks Graph validation and preparation")
        H("fal:fa-link Host binding and parameter resolver")
        Q("fal:fa-list-ordered Coalesced graph-change queue")
        D("fal:fa-package hdUE delegate")
    end
    subgraph Unreal["fal:fa-boxes Unreal Engine"]
        X("fal:fa-library Prepared MaterialX library")
        E("fal:fa-blend UE Substrate material expressions")
        C("fal:fa-database Cooked materials and Builder library")
        W("fal:fa-hammer Background editor compile / cook")
        I("fal:fa-archive Immutable packages<br/>with inline shader code")
        B("fal:fa-boxes UE backend in the same process")
    end
    R("fal:fa-image Lumen / Path Tracer color AOV")
    V --> A --> U --> P
    X --> P
    P --> E --> C
    U --> H
    C --> H
    H --> D --> B --> R
    H --> Q --> W --> I --> B
    W --> H

    classDef host stroke-width:1px
    classDef hdue stroke-width:1px
    classDef unreal stroke-width:1px
    classDef output stroke-width:1px

    class Houdini,V,A,U host
    class Delegate,P,H,Q,D hdue
    class Unreal,X,E,C,W,I,B unreal
    class R output

Houdini supplies the node editor, connections, parameters, and undo. hdUE exports its own typed graph. The Builder nodes are not a VEX implementation of Substrate and do not create a Karma material.

items.title: Authoring in Houdini
items.text:
The hdUE Substrate VOPs ship in integrations/houdini/otls/hdue_substrate.hda, so they are in the TAB menu's hdUE submenu from startup, in /mat and inside a Material Library LOP, in the folders UE's Material Editor palette files the matching expressions under: Substrate (every Substrate expression, as in UE), Parameters, Constants, Math, Coordinates, Texture, Utility and Volume (CATEGORY in scripts/build_substrate_hda.py). Like Karma's and MaterialX's VOPs (kma_*, hmtlx*), they are locked external-shader leaf nodes (hdue::substrate_<kind>::1.3, no network inside): Slabs, layers and mixes are surface shaders, the others generic. Each carries a render mask (hdUE) by which Solaris picks its shader translator, here integrations/houdini/husdplugins/shadertranslators/hdue.py.

hdUE Substrate Material Builder is the material, made the way SideFX makes the Karma Material Builder. That one is no asset: the TAB tool vop_karmamtlxsubnet ($HFS/houdini/toolbar/ExtraTools.shelf, TAB menu > Karma wherever a Material Builder can go) calls voptoolutils.createMaskedMtlXSubnet, which creates a plain VOP subnet, adds its Material Builder parameters (tabmenumask, shader_rendercontextname, shader_forcechildren, the USD class inherit controls), fills it with a starter network and turns its material flag on. The tool vop_hduesubstratebuilder (integrations/houdini/toolbar/hdUE.shelf, TAB menu > hdUE in /mat and Material Library LOPs, and the hdUE shelf) does the same through hdue_substrate.tool: an editable subnet with the same parameters (render context hdue, TAB menu mask hdUE subnetconnector: the hdUE Substrate nodes and the output connector, the only nodes it translates), a Slab wired to a surface output connector, and the material flag. Its render context is what marks a subnet as a builder (hdue_substrate.is_builder). Put it in a Material Library LOP, or leave it in /mat and point the library's Material VOP at it. The library authors the builder as one USD material (the graph described below), assigns it like any other material, and re-authors it on parameter edits, rewiring and node changes. No Python LOP is involved.

The hdUE shelf provides:

  • hdUE Substrate Material Builder: create a builder (in /mat from the shelf).
  • Water Coating Example: create a builder with a MaterialX base, clear water Slab, public coverage/roughness parameters, float mask, Weight, and Vertical Layer.
  • Author Substrate USD: add a Material Library LOP after the displayed LOP that authors the selected builder at /Looks/<builder name>, bound to the current Scene Graph selection.

The same operations are available in Houdini's Python shell:

import hou
import hdue_substrate

library = hou.node("/stage/materiallibrary1")
builder = hdue_substrate.create(parent=library)

# Optional example; set the MaterialX Surface node to an existing USD material.
water = hdue_substrate.create(preset="wet", material="/Looks/Base")
hdue_substrate.author_lop(water, "/Looks/Water", hou.node("/stage/sphere1"), ["/sphere1"])

author_lop(builder, material_path, input_node, prim_paths) configures the builder's own Material Library, or adds one after input_node that references a builder elsewhere. Source USD files and referenced materials remain independently editable. Scenes saved with the earlier Python authoring LOP keep working; that LOP still calls hdue_substrate.cook().

scripts/build_substrate_hda.py builds the leaf VOPs from scripts/substrate_graph.py, with the help of each node and parameter: run it after editing either and commit the result. The type names (hdue::substrate_<kind>::1.3) are unchanged, so earlier scenes load the shipped definitions.

Builders saved before the Material Builder subnet are instances of the asset hdue::substrate_builder::1.3. integrations/houdini/otls/hdue_substrate_builder_legacy.hda keeps that definition, deprecated in OPcustomize (out of the TAB menu), so those scenes load, author and render unchanged. hdue_substrate.upgrade(node) turns one into a Material Builder subnet with the same name, network and parameters on its nodes.

items.title: Graph rules
items.text:
Surface connections use native VOP BSDF sockets. Numeric connections use float/vector sockets. The exporter validates its own port types and rejects unsupported implicit conversions or unrecognized VOP nodes.

Unconnected inputs take UE's own defaults (each node's Compile in MaterialExpressionSubstrate.cpp). Unlit, Hair, Eye and Single Layer Water must be the graph's output: UE's Substrate does not let an operator combine them. Multi-output nodes connect by output name. samples/substrate/bsdfs.usda holds one material per node above the Slab; Prepare-Substrate.ps1 -InputUsd on it compiles and cooks them all, and the script fails when UE's cook rejects a material (its shader compile, where Substrate's graph rules apply).

The first graph format allows up to 256 connected nodes, one MaterialX Surface input, and one Float Mask Primvar node. Disconnected serialized nodes, cycles, incompatible ports, missing surface inputs, duplicate public names, reserved HdUE_ parameter names, and non-finite numeric data are errors. Unconnected VOP work-in-progress branches are excluded from export.

items.title: Direct texture connections
items.text:
Texture Sample can connect its RGB (out) output directly to a Slab's Diffuse Albedo or F0. Connect its RGBA output to Extract Channel for packed roughness or coverage masks; alternatively use its individual R/G/B/A outputs. Image masks can drive Substrate Weight and mix inputs without a float-primvar overlay.

Use srgb for ordinary color images and raw for roughness, masks, and encoded tangent-space normal maps. A Normal Map node decodes RGB from [0, 1] to [-1, 1], scales XY by Strength, and normalizes the result. Flip Green defaults to enabled for OpenGL/MaterialX +Y maps because the mesh bridge converts V to UE's texture convention. Disable it for DirectX -Y maps. Connect the converted result to Slab Normal. Connecting an sRGB Texture Sample directly to Normal Map is rejected. Raw sources retain RGB/alpha using UE's uncompressed vector-displacement texture setting; this favors data fidelity over texture memory savings.

UV Coordinates applies UV0 * Scale + Offset in UE texture coordinates, after the mesh bridge's st V conversion. An unconnected Texture Sample UV uses UV0. Only the transported UV0 set is available; other indices are rejected. Scale and offset are live two-component parameters. Missing mesh UVs cannot supply a meaningful texture layout.

The file parameter uses Houdini's file picker and expands variables such as $HIP. VOP-relative paths are anchored to the HIP folder before USD export. USD stores the file as an asset attribute, so referenced layers retain their source-layer-relative resolution. Preparation snapshots the image inputs into its output folder, imports texture assets, and compiles materials that reference them. Color-space or address-mode variants get separate prepared texture assets.

An explicit BaseName.<UDIM>.ext or BaseName_<UDIM>.ext pattern imports all matching tiles. Multi-tile inputs use streaming virtual textures. Tile indices, source-block coordinates, membership, and source content are checked. A single tile must be 1001 and uses an ordinary 2D texture; a single off-origin tile is rejected. A literal numbered file remains a single 2D image. Existing virtual-texture residency checks gate Path Tracer accumulation. Direct Builder op: / opdef: image inputs require baking/exporting to image files first; the separate existing COP/MaterialX resolver does not automatically export these new nodes.

The direct texture example has one mesh and one composite material. An sRGB checker drives albedo, packed raw G drives roughness, packed raw A controls the top Slab's coverage, and a raw RGB image passes through Normal Map to the base Slab. NormalStrength is a live Scalar Parameter. No MaterialX base library is required for this scene.

.\scripts\Prepare-Substrate.ps1 `
  -InputUsd samples/substrate/textures.usda `
  -OutputDirectory out/textures-prepared

scripts/generate_substrate_textures.py creates the owned image fixtures and USD scene. Its optional HIP output places the editable builder inside a Material Library LOP, which authors and binds it.

To create a HIP from the existing supplied scene without regenerating its images, run the generator through the configured Houdini Python executable:

. ./scripts/Local-Paths.ps1
$HoudiniPython = Join-Path (Get-HdUELocalPath houdini_root) 'bin/hython.exe'
uv run -- $HoudiniPython scripts/generate_substrate_textures.py `
  --scene samples/substrate/textures.usda `
  --hip out/texture-example.hip `
  --runtime-config .local/builder-runtime.json

The runtime profile must select the prepared library and a staged runtime containing its cooked assets. Generated HIPs retain the source image paths used for preparation.

items.title: USD representation and identity
items.text:
A Builder material has unreal:substrate:version = 1. Its outputs:unreal:surface connects to a typed USD Shader graph below the material. Shader identifiers have the form unreal:substrate:slab, unreal:substrate:vertical, or unreal:substrate:scalar. An ordinary Preview Surface output supplies a basic fallback before preparation.

MaterialX Surface inputs use a relationship to the source USD Material. USD composition remaps that relationship when the enclosing asset is referenced below another root. A plain string containing an absolute prim path would not provide that behavior.

Graph signatures include operators, wiring, public parameter names, and static options such as parameter blending and subsurface mode. Numeric/color input values, Float/Color Constant values, UV scale/offset, Normal Map Flip Green, Extract Channel selection, Float Mask Primvar fallback values, public scalar/color values, and the selected mask name are excluded from the structural signature. The editor emits scalar/vector material parameters with stable reserved HdUE_Auto_ names for automatic inputs. The host updates these values on material instances. Connected inputs continue to evaluate their upstream nodes; their unconnected fallback fields do not override a connection. The prepared MaterialX input has a separate dependency identity; replacing its graph or imported dependencies requires preparing the composite material again.

Texture asset paths, color space, address mode, UV set index, and selected output sockets remain static graph inputs. Source hashes and UDIM membership are stored in the prepared library and checked when loading it. Replacing an image or changing its tile set requires preparing, cooking, and staging again; filenames are not runtime texture parameters.

Automatic parameters use compiler version 2 in preparation manifests and libraries; version 3 adds the ID-pass switch (AOVs) and Nanite usage to every prepared material. Previously prepared materials must be rebuilt, cooked, and staged once to obtain the generated parameters. A library from the earlier compiler produces an explicit preparation message instead of accepting value edits that its cooked shader cannot apply. Existing USD graphs and editable VOP assets retain their graph schema version.

The generated Builder library records the graph signature, MaterialX dependency identity, cooked material, and cooked mask-preview material. It is local generated data and belongs outside Git.

items.title: Preparation, cook, and launch
items.text:
Configure the SDK and engine locations in ignored local configuration as described in the repository README. Prepare the MaterialX input before composing it in a Builder graph. For the supplied example:

.\scripts\Import-MaterialX.ps1 `
  -Source @('samples/materialx/standard_surface.mtlx', 'samples/materialx/open_pbr_surface.mtlx') `
  -Destination /Game/HdUE/BuilderBase `
  -OutputDirectory out/builder-base -SkipCook

.\scripts\Prepare-Substrate.ps1 `
  -InputUsd samples/substrate/contrast.usda `
  -MaterialXLibrary out/builder-base/library.json `
  -OutputDirectory out/builder-prepared

.\scripts\Build-Backend.ps1
.\scripts\Build-Houdini.ps1 -BuildDirectory build/houdini-substrate
.\scripts\Stage-Runtime.ps1 -OutputDirectory out/builder-runtime

Choose fresh preparation output directories. Prepare-Substrate.ps1 exports and validates the USD graphs, runs the HdUESubstrate commandlet, builds a library from its receipts, and cooks the generated assets. -SkipBuild and -SkipCook are available for controlled iteration. This remains the initial/manual preparation path; Solaris topology edits can use the background path below.

Save an ignored .local/builder-runtime.json profile. Relative paths are resolved from the profile's directory:

{
  "version": 1,
  "backend_dll": "../out/builder-runtime/Windows/HdUEBackend/Binaries/Win64/HdUEBackend.dll",
  "runtime_project": "../out/builder-runtime/Windows/HdUEBackend/HdUEBackend.uproject",
  "materialx_library": "../out/builder-base/library.json",
  "substrate_library": "../out/builder-prepared/library.json"
}

Launch a new host process with the staged backend/runtime project and both libraries:

.\scripts\Launch-Houdini.ps1 `
  -RuntimeConfig .local/builder-runtime.json `
  -BuildDirectory build/houdini-substrate `
  -InputUsd samples/substrate/contrast.usda `
  -MaterialXLibrary out/builder-base/library.json `
  -SubstrateLibrary out/builder-prepared/library.json

The local runtime profile selects backend_dll and runtime_project. Its optional materialx_library and substrate_library keys provide default library selections. Solaris exposes Cooked MaterialX Library and Prepared Substrate Library as render settings (unreal:materialxLibrary, unreal:substrateLibrary, hdUE Render Settings > Rendering > Materials), and the mask-preview toggle in the hdUE settings subnet. husk applies them as the viewport does: the delegate runs the same library code on the stage it renders (hdue_batch.py, through Houdini's Python) before each frame, preparing a graph that is unprepared or changed since its preparation (or, with automatic preparation off, failing the frame with the library's message instead of rendering a fallback). usdview takes --hdue-substrate-library (else the profile's) and syncs it after the MaterialX library. Staging into a fresh folder preserves the binaries used by an existing host.

The standalone host accepts a resolved settings snapshot generated by scripts/prepare_renderer_settings.py --substrate-library .... Pass that file to Test-Hydra.ps1 -RendererSettings or hdue_usd_render --renderer-settings. Regenerate the snapshot after changing the authored Builder settings; live VOP editing is handled by Solaris.

items.title: Editing and rendering
items.text:
Edit Required work Numeric/color input value on any node, including Slab color/F0/roughness/MFP, Weight/Mix, and layer thickness Update generated native material parameters and start a new render generation UV scale/offset, Normal Map strength/Flip Green, Extract Channel selection, constant value, or Float Mask fallback Update generated native material parameters and start a new render generation Scalar Parameter or Color Parameter value Update public native material parameters and start a new render generation Float Mask Primvar name or samples Resolve/re-expand the selected mask and update the relevant color buffers Mesh topology, material binding, or transform Synchronize the affected scene resources and matching mask revision Node type, wiring, public parameter name, subsurface mode, or blending option Background compilation/cook and material replacement in Solaris; manual preparation elsewhere MaterialX source graph or imported texture dependencies Re-prepare the MaterialX input and its Builder material Builder image path, color space, or address mode Background preparation in Solaris when the graph signature changes Image bytes or UDIM membership changed without a USD graph edit Manually refresh preparation; file contents alone do not invalidate the topology cache

Public parameters are shared by prims bound to the same USD material. Masks vary independently on each mesh or material-binding GeomSubset. Use separate material instances/material prims when independently authored public parameter values are needed.

The Material Library LOP depends on the builder's parameters and wiring natively, also for a builder in /mat: value edits and bursts of structural edits settle through Houdini's scheduler at the next evaluation, in one cook. (Saved Python authoring LOPs track rewiring through a hidden revision parameter instead.)

An edit that requires preparation pauses the current request and reports progress in Houdini's status bar. The last valid displayed AOV remains visible, but the pending request exposes no completed frame. Identical statuses are published once per session instead of being resubmitted on every material poll. Successful background preparation or restoring a cached graph resumes rendering.

Disconnecting a required surface or output is represented by an unreal:substrate:authoringError material attribute while retaining a valid LOP stage. It pauses the requested material without terminating the host timer or starting an invalid compiler job. Reconnecting clears that attribute and resumes validation. A valid topology change, including disconnecting an optional numeric input, is prepared in the background. Disconnected inputs explicitly clear weaker USD connections so the original source/reference cannot silently reconnect them. Unrelated LOP stage-read errors are recoverable and do not terminate UE ticking.

items.title: Background graph preparation in Solaris
items.text:
Prepare Edited Materials (unreal:substrateAutoPrepare, named before it also covered MaterialX graphs; hdUE Render Settings > Rendering > Materials, on by default) is a render setting, read alike by the viewport and husk: the viewport prepares graphs as you edit them, and husk prepares the graphs a frame needs before rendering it (the same worker, without the edit debounce; the frame waits for it). Off, an unprepared graph shows the library's message in the viewport and fails a husk frame. An older hdUE settings subnet's Prepare graph edits automatically toggle is still read when the render setting is unset. Retry material preparation retries a failed graph after correcting a missing source or toolchain problem.

The worker requires the configured OpenUSD SDK, uv-managed Python runtime, UE editor, and a previously built HdUESubstrate commandlet in this repository's backend project. The worker uses standalone USD Python with isolated plugin paths so the GUI host's Houdini USD environment cannot leak into preparation. It snapshots only typed material graphs and their resolved base-material identities; geometry is not copied to the worker. Graph edits settle briefly before a single worker starts. Editor/cook work is serialized for this checkout, and only the latest requested graph is queued while a previous job is running.

A job (Prepare-LiveMaterials.ps1) is one Python run that writes its graphs (live_materials.py export), one editor that imports its MaterialX graphs through UE's importer, compiles its Substrate Builder graphs (HdUESubstrate -GraphList=, their shaders together at the end) and cooks them all with UE's own cook commandlet (-RunAsCookCommandlet -CookAfter, after rescanning the new packages into the asset registry), then one Python run that writes the library and publishes (live_materials.py finish). The viewport's jobs also compile each material's mask-preview variant; husk's skip it, since only the viewport's wet-mask preview uses it, so a husk result is used by husk and the viewport prepares the graph again with its preview. 16 graphs took 18 s to compile where one editor run per graph took 163 s, and husk prepares 8 materials and renders in 22 s (8 s of it the render; 37 s with a separate cook editor and no preview skip): of the 14 s of preparation, the editor's start-up takes 7.6 s, the Python steps about 5 s and the cook 1.4 s, with shaders from the cache. Each published job's library is written beside its packages (hdue-live-library.json) and loaded by every later process on that runtime, viewport or husk, so a graph is prepared once per runtime (once per farm when render nodes share it), not once per frame or task: the second husk render of the same 8 materials took 8 s.

Every preparing process cleans the live content in the background when it starts (live_materials.clean): interrupted publishes after an hour; jobs without a library or no longer valid, and jobs a newer job fully replaces, after a day; jobs no process has used for 30 days (a library's modification time records its last use); worker folders in the log directory after 7 days. A job's intermediate cook output is deleted once it is published. Files a running UE holds open stay until a later clean-up. Each result uses a fresh /Game/HdUE/Live/... package namespace. A focused cook writes to an isolated output directory with material shader-code sharing disabled. Shader code is embedded in the new cooked packages, so the active runtime's already-open shared shader libraries are never replaced. The completed payload is atomically added to the staged runtime's loose Content directory; the current generic material binding API loads the new material and creates its runtime instances. This path requires writable, loose cooked content on the supported Windows runtime. It does not update pak/IoStore deployments or arbitrary external editor projects.

The running UE instance continues ticking while the editor compiles. The resolver binds a result only when it matches the current USD graph. Superseded results can enter the variant cache but cannot replace a newer edit. Public and generated parameter values are read from the latest USD state after compilation, preserving value edits made while the job was running. Returning to a prepared/cached topology does not start another cook. Path Tracer starts a new generation after replacement and the existing material/texture readiness checks.

Compilation is asynchronous rather than instantaneous. Progress and failures appear in Houdini's status bar, runtime-state.json, and the session's substrate-live output directory. Failed graphs retain the last valid display and retry on a different topology or the retry button. In-flight editor jobs are allowed to finish their immutable output if the host closes. Generated variants are cached for the process and are not automatically unloaded or deleted.

Runtime material instances retain the prepared graph and its base texture parameters. Per-mesh mask instances are isolated. The surface C ABI functions copy caller data, validates the session and geometry revision, and publishes updates on the owner thread. A mask-selector edit can fetch a newly selected primvar from the synchronized Hydra delegate using cached triangulation, without requiring a geometry upload.

Path Tracer accumulation is reset after relevant edits. It starts after material/mask publication and required virtual-texture residency are ready. Older image generations are discarded. A missing mask or unprepared graph produces a specific error and does not qualify as a completed render of the requested material.

items.title: Float masks
items.text:
The initial transport reserves the dynamic mesh color overlay's red channel. Values are linear normalized data in [0, 1], with no sRGB conversion. GPU color storage may quantize to 8 bits; this is a mask transport, not a general unbounded-float primvar implementation.

Supported inputs are float scalar constant primvars and float-array constant, uniform, vertex/varying, or face-varying primvars. Indexed arrays are flattened before use. Triangulation and GeomSubset partitioning preserve the source domains and face discontinuities. A configured missing primvar, invalid count/type/index, or NaN/Inf is an error. An empty name uses the node's compiled default value.

Mask-only updates use color-buffer notifications. They do not upload positions, indices, normals, or UVs. Topology changes create a new geometry revision; updates targeting an obsolete revision are rejected.

items.title: Volume materials
items.text:
A builder whose output is a Substrate Volumetric Fog Cloud (hdue_substrate.create(preset="volume")) is a volume material: it authors UsdShade's volume terminal (outputs:unreal:volume, no Preview Surface) and prepares into a UE material of the Volume domain, used with heterogeneous volumes, whose front material is UE's SubstrateVolumetricFogCloudBSDF (the closure UE's heterogeneous volumes read with Substrate, HeterogeneousVolumesLiveShadingUtils.ush). Bound to a Volume prim (a material binding, as on meshes), it replaces hdUE's default M_HdUEVolume in the Houdini viewport, husk and usdview.

The backend gives it what it gives M_HdUEVolume: the volume's density grid and the field primvars:unreal:emissionField names as the 3D textures Density and Emission, the WorldToUVW0..2 rows placing them, and the ExtinctionScale, TemperatureScale and EmissionIntensity scalars. Volume Field samples one of the two grids; left unconnected, the Fog Cloud's extinction is the density times ExtinctionScale and its emission the BlackBody of the emission field, so an unedited volume graph renders as M_HdUEVolume does. Its numeric inputs update live as on surfaces. samples/volume_material/volume_material.usda and the in-Houdini test -TestKind volume-material check both: the default graph against M_HdUEVolume, and a live albedo edit.

items.title: Decal materials
items.text: A builder whose output is a Substrate Convert To Decal (hdue_substrate.create(preset="decal"): the Slab, converted) is a decal material: it prepares into a UE material of the Deferred Decal domain, translucent (UE's DBuffer decals, which Substrate requires), whose front material is UE's SubstrateConvertToDecal of the surface wired to it, with Coverage as its opacity. Bound to an UnrealDecal prim, it is that decal's material in Houdini's viewport, husk and usdview (decals).

items.title: Water coating example
items.text:
Use samples/substrate/contrast.usda for visual comparison. All three spheres share the composite material, with masks of 0, 1, and a split transition. The base MaterialX coat is overridden to 0 and its specular roughness to 0.65; the water roughness remains 0.08. This makes the change in reflection width easier to inspect while preserving the base color. scripts/generate_substrate_comparison.py generates the scene and can optionally create a Material Library HIP or a single-mesh variant. Published base-parameter overrides use the existing prepared library and do not require a new shader cook.

The older showcase.usda uses a base with coat weight 0.9 and coat roughness 0.07. Its water layer has similar roughness, so the three coated/checker surfaces can look similar. Controlled same-camera coverage-0/coverage-1 renders confirm that the effect changes the image; similar appearance alone does not establish a missing binding. The original scene remains useful for the existing-coat regression.

The three spheres represent dry, uniformly coated, and masked results. Each coated sphere evaluates its base BSDF and water Slab inside one composite material on that mesh. The water layer does not require a second geometric surface. The older showcase's Ramp sphere also contains a GeomSubset binding regression; any backend partitioning for that subset is independent of Slab layering. The contrast scene has no GeomSubsets. A single-mesh inspection variant has also been verified with one rendered mesh and one assigned material in both Lumen and 64-sample Path Tracer output.

The supplied network places a clear dielectric Slab above the original MaterialX front material. It uses IOR 1.33 converted to F0, roughness 0.08, a mean free path large enough to avoid an artistic absorption tint, and a 0.01 cm top-layer thickness. Coverage is the product of the saturated public amount and the float mask. The base normal-map graph is retained; the top slab uses the mesh shading normal unless another normal is connected.

These values belong to the example graph. Artists can change its nodes, expose additional parameters, or construct another surface entirely. Layer thickness is expressed in UE centimeters and is independent of the USD stage's meters-per-unit setting.

items.title: Limits and validation
items.text:
The current backend uses Adaptive GBuffer with a four-closure, 128-byte-per-pixel budget. The owned MaterialX water example compiles to three closures and 92 bytes per pixel; its base compiles to two closures and 64 bytes. Arbitrarily complex graphs require separate qualification. Parameter blending is an explicit authored choice.

Initial support covers opaque graphs on generic USD meshes. Native uasset material slots, arbitrary UE material expressions, multiple MaterialX bases, multiple float-primvar mask channels, unbounded float buffers, full transmission/glass authoring, displacement, volume fields other than density and the emission field, and compiling shaders inside the rendering DLL are outside this implementation. Existing prepared MaterialX textures remain on the imported graph. Direct Texture Samples additionally support image masks; Float Mask Primvar continues to use the separate per-mesh overlay transport. Additional UV sets, direct COP/opdef baking, and dedicated BC5 normal-map compression are outside the direct-texture implementation. Background topology preparation currently targets Solaris and this repository's loose-content backend runtime.

Current checks cover typed graph validation, float32 USD round trips, remapped MaterialX relationships, native VOP-to-USD parameter updates, both SDK builds, and Lumen/64-sample Path Tracer output through repeated delegate sessions. The eight-case Solaris regression passes public coverage/roughness edits, preparation-error recovery after a structural edit is reverted, mask-only updates, and preview restoration. Generated logs, images, shader receipts, and HIP files remain under ignored output directories. No hardware-independent performance target is claimed.

Direct textures additionally pass 18 numerical color-AOV checks across Lumen and 64-sample Path Tracer: sRGB versus raw values, all four extracted channels, the direct alpha socket, and two UDIM tiles selected using UV offsets. The 15-image Solaris regression verifies direct Slab values, live UV transforms, channel selection, Flip Green, both render modes, settled preparation errors, required/optional wire disconnects, reconnection, and live edits after reconnection. A 100-edit burst produces one authoring cook in the headless dependency test and at most two in the Solaris regression, without geometry/mask uploads. The native host self-test verifies that a preparation error stops the render-pass update loop without publishing a completed frame and that clearing the error resumes it. The direct-texture example compiles to two closures and 52 bytes per pixel on the tested configuration.

The eight-case background-topology regression passes node addition, generated parameter updates on the new material, Lumen and 64-sample Path Tracer replacement, a newer edit queued during compilation, rejection of superseded display results, cached topology restoration, and incomplete-connection recovery. Three worker jobs complete with the same Houdini process, Hydra session, and one UE initialization. Unit checks cover single-flight queue ordering, failure/retry behavior, worker environment isolation, and atomic publication without replacing an existing live package directory.

Implementation entry points:

  • VOP network reading and authoring
  • VOP definitions and help
  • Material Library shader translator
  • Typed graph and USD contract
  • Texture resolution and preparation
  • Numerical texture/UV/UDIM render checks
  • Background queue and variant cache
  • Isolated import/compile/cook worker
  • Same-process topology regression
  • Preparation command
  • UE expression compiler
  • Runtime library resolver
  • Solaris regression

items.title: Wet surface internals
items.text:
The user guide is Wet surfaces. The wet profile is implemented as specified below: Import-MaterialX.ps1 -WetProfile runs HdUEPrepareWetMaterials (unreal/HdUEBackend/Source/HdUEContent/Private/WetMaterials.cpp), which duplicates each imported opaque Substrate material into a _Wet_v1 variant (a clear Slab with F0 from IOR 1.33, HdUE_WetRoughness 0.08, mean free path 10^6, Weight by HdUE_WetAmount and the mask, Vertical Layer 0.01 cm, no parameter blending) and a _WetMask_v1 preview variant, and records them as the library entry's surface_effects.wet (scripts/build_materialx_library.py rejects Standard Surface/OpenPBR materials with active subsurface, transmission or sheen). scripts/surface_effects.py resolves the unreal:surface:wet:* opinions per Mesh and GeomSubset after composition and validates the masks; integrations/houdini/python3.13libs/hdue_surface.py authors them on a Render Geometry Settings LOP; the delegate sends the bindings through apply_surfaces (src/hydra/delegate.cpp, src/hydra/wet_mask.h). Substrate Builder graphs with a Float Mask Primvar use the same surface binding path (graph flag).

What follows is the original Draft 0.1 specification, kept for its requirements and acceptance criteria. The Substrate Builder generalises the coating into an authored graph.

The first release adds a thin water coating above a prepared MaterialX surface. Artists control its coverage on USD meshes with a scalar amount and an optional float primvar authored in Houdini. The base material, its bindings, and referenced source files remain independently editable.

The agreed starting scope is a Substrate coating, MaterialX materials on generic USD meshes, and float primvar masks. The detailed defaults and interfaces below are proposed implementation contracts.

items.title: User workflow
items.text:
1. Prepare a MaterialX library with the wet profile enabled, then cook and stage the resulting materials.
  2. Load the USD scene in the existing hdUE host and select the matching library.
  3. Enable the wet effect on a Mesh or an ancestor Xform. Choose a mask primvar or apply a uniform amount.
  4. Edit the amount, coating roughness, or primvar values while inspecting Lumen or Path Tracer output.
  5. Disable the effect to return to the original prepared material.

A graph/profile change requires preparation, cook, staging, and runtime restart. Amount, roughness, mask values, and placement changes do not require shader compilation. The existing same-process host and UE lifetime remain in use.

items.title: First release scope
items.text:
Area Contract Base surfaces Prepared Standard Surface and OpenPBR reflection materials with opaque blend mode Base details Preserve base color, metallic response, roughness, existing coat, normal maps, and prepared UDIMs Geometry Generic USD meshes, material-binding GeomSubsets, and expanded instanceable references Mask input Uniform amount, or a named float primvar on the target mesh Rendering Lumen and Path Tracer using the same generated material graph Coating count One wet coating above the entire original surface graph

Subsurface/fuzz profiles, transmission/glass, masked/translucent blend modes, hair/eye shaders, arbitrary cooked uasset materials, native asset material slots, image/COP/UDIM masks, puddle geometry, droplets, animated ripples, absorption tint, and thin-film interference are deferred. Existing normal and UDIM textures in the base material remain supported; the new wet mask itself is a float primvar.

Only qualified base graphs are accepted. Preparation records the supported capabilities and validates the combined graph against the backend's closure and storage budgets. An incompatible graph produces a specific error rather than substituting a cheaper material without notice.

items.title: Water coating model
items.text:
The graph retains the original Substrate front-material expression as its bottom input. A clear dielectric Slab forms the top input. Substrate Coverage Weight controls the top slab's coverage, and Substrate Vertical Layer composes it above the bottom graph. These are graph operators; this design does not depend on the Material Layers authoring UI. Epic Substrate overview

The proposed wet profile has:

  • A fixed interface IOR of 1.33, converted to the appropriate Substrate reflectance input during preparation.
  • Clear transmission through the coating, with no artistic absorption tint or diffuse water lobe.
  • A fixed coating thickness of 0.1 mm, converted to 0.01 cm for the UE graph. Stage units and object scale do not change this profile thickness.
  • An editable coating roughness, default 0.08.
  • The interpolated mesh shading normal for the coating. The bottom graph retains its original normal-map evaluation; the coating does not flatten or overwrite that graph.

The amount describes fractional surface coverage, not water depth. The final coverage is:

coverage = saturate(amount) * saturate(mask)

An empty mask name selects a constant mask of 1. Coverage 0 selects the dry surface; coverage 1 applies the full coating. Intermediate values expose both dry and coated surface areas through the Substrate coverage operator. No automatic base-color darkening is added in this release.

Parameter blending is disabled in the first shader proof of concept so that the coating remains a separate slab. The implementation must verify that compilation retains the intended layering within the configured budgets. The current backend uses four closures and 128 bytes per pixel; an original material already consuming its budget may not accept another slab. Automatic budget increases and silent simplification are outside this release.

items.title: USD authoring contract
items.text:
The following attributes are authored on a Mesh, its material-binding GeomSubset, or an ancestor Xform/Scope. They are renderer-specific settings and do not modify the MaterialX graph.

Attribute Type Default Meaning unreal:surface:wet:enabled bool false Enable the wet profile for the target binding unreal:surface:wet:amount float 1 Overall coverage multiplier, in [0, 1] unreal:surface:wet:roughness float 0.08 Roughness of the water coating, in [0, 1] unreal:surface:wet:maskPrimvar token empty Primvar base name, for example wetness, without primvars:

hdUE resolves each setting from the nearest authored opinion, starting at a subset, then its mesh, then ancestors, followed by the default. This is an explicit hdUE ancestor search: ordinary custom USD attributes do not acquire this inheritance automatically. Normal USD composition determines the winning opinion at each prim. Values may be time sampled.

A child enabled = false disables an inherited effect. An explicitly empty mask name requests uniform coverage even when a parent selected a mask. Settings on a referenced asset's placement prim apply to its contained supported meshes without editing the referenced file. Masks are evaluated on the owning mesh, including when a subset selects a different mask name.

This override-layer example assumes an existing four-point mesh with a prepared MaterialX binding:

#usda 1.0

over "World"
{
    over "Asset"
    {
        custom bool unreal:surface:wet:enabled = true
        custom float unreal:surface:wet:amount = 0.8
        custom float unreal:surface:wet:roughness = 0.08
        custom token unreal:surface:wet:maskPrimvar = "wetness"

        over "Panel"
        {
            float[] primvars:wetness = [0, 0, 1, 1] (
                interpolation = "vertex"
            )
        }
    }
}

items.title: Mask interpretation
items.text:
Accept float scalar constant primvars and float-array constant, uniform, vertex/varying, and face-varying primvars. Indexed primvars must be resolved before use. Standard inherited constant primvars may be used when supplied by the USD/Hydra delegate. Values are linear data and receive no color-space conversion.

Resolve masks against the original USD face and point domains, then triangulate and partition with the same mapping used for geometry. GeomSubset splits must preserve mask values on the appropriate triangles, including discontinuities at face-varying boundaries. Generated normals and material boundaries must not change the mask's meaning.

Clamp finite samples to [0, 1]. Reject a requested missing primvar, an unsupported type/interpolation, invalid indices/counts, and NaN/Inf values. An unconfigured mask is uniform; a configured but missing mask is an error.

The proposed first GPU transport is a reserved red channel in the dynamic mesh's color overlay. It must not overwrite authored USD displayColor or its material semantics. CPU values remain float; normalized 8-bit GPU storage is acceptable for this release, with mask error no greater than 1/255 before shading interpolation. If the backend cannot preserve these linear values, the mask transport proof of concept must select another representation before integration.

Mask-only changes update attribute buffers rather than resending positions, topology, normals, and UVs. A topology edit re-expands the mask and associates it with the new geometry revision. An update for an obsolete revision is rejected.

items.title: Preparation and material identity
items.text:
Preparation generates a wet-capable material variant for each eligible base graph. The variant connects the original front material below the water slab and publishes reserved wet amount, roughness, and mask-selection parameters. Original published MaterialX parameter bindings remain available on the variant.

The library gains an additive, versioned wet-profile capability record containing the profile version, cooked variant asset, base identity, parameter mapping, mask transport, and validation results. Libraries without that record continue to render their base materials but cannot claim wet-profile support.

The variant cache key includes the base graph/static inputs and dependencies, wet-profile version, backend/engine shader configuration, and target platform. It excludes prim paths, amount, roughness, and mask sample values. Machine-specific source locations stay in ignored local configuration and generated registries.

At runtime, a mesh/subset binding receives its own effect instance identity scoped to the session and rendered object. Two prims sharing one USD material may use different wet settings without changing one another. The compiled variant and base textures may be shared; mutable material state and masks must remain isolated. Removing a prim or recreating a delegate releases its effect resources.

A disabled effect or uniform zero amount binds the original dry material. Removing an effect restores the original binding. A mixed mask uses the generated coating graph, including at pixels where the mask is zero.

items.title: Runtime synchronization
items.text:
flowchart LR
    M("fal:fa-file-code MaterialX source")
    U("fal:fa-sliders-horizontal USD settings and float primvar")
    subgraph Unreal["fal:fa-boxes Unreal Engine"]
        P("fal:fa-hammer Editor preparation and cook")
        V("fal:fa-droplets Cooked wet variant and library")
        B("fal:fa-boxes UE backend in the host process")
    end
    H("fal:fa-package Hydra resolution and mesh partitioning")
    R("fal:fa-image Lumen or Path Tracer color AOV")
    M --> P --> V --> B
    U --> H
    H -->|"Versioned C ABI"| B
    B --> R

    classDef host stroke-width:1px
    classDef hdue stroke-width:1px
    classDef unreal stroke-width:1px
    classDef output stroke-width:1px

    class M,U host
    class H hdue
    class Unreal,P,V,B unreal
    class R output

The host/preparation adapter resolves the authored USD settings after reference composition and supplies an explicit effect-binding map to the delegate. Custom USD attributes are not assumed to appear automatically in HdSceneDelegate::Get. Each host must supply the same resolved contract through its renderer-settings or scene adapter. The delegate reads the selected mask primvar through Hydra and expands it with the geometry. A mask-name change must invalidate the relevant primvar data even when point positions are unchanged.

Parallel Sync work is accumulated into batches. The owner thread validates and applies each batch, then the render thread consumes the resulting resources.

Effect bindings and mask updates go through the surface functions of the ABI table (apply_surfaces, get_surface_status in include/hdue/bridge.h) with fixed-width fields, caller-owned data, a session handle, and a geometry revision. Scalar/vector updates reuse the material parameter facilities where possible.

For each affected binding, validate the complete material/mask update before publishing it. Copy caller data during the call. Never expose UE/USD objects across the boundary.

Amount, roughness, mask, binding, topology, and relevant time changes advance the render generation and invalidate Path Tracer accumulation. Camera-only motion must not rebuild/cook a material or upload an unchanged mask. Geometry updates must retain or reapply the matching mask.

Path Tracer begins a new accumulation only after the effect instance, mask upload, and all required base-material virtual-texture residency are ready. Existing generation checks discard stale images. Time is held fixed during accumulation.

items.title: UI and diagnostics
items.text:
Solaris exposes an authoring control for a prim selection: enable, amount, roughness, and mask primvar. hdue_surface.create() adds a Render Geometry Settings LOP (hdUE_wet_surface) whose Primitives are the selected paths and whose hdUE tab sets the four unreal:surface:wet:* attributes (Set or Create, coating on); any Render Geometry Settings LOP can author them the same way. This writes an override layer on the selected prim paths, rather than changing a shared USD material. Authoring and undo stay on the Houdini UI thread. usdview/standalone may consume the same authored attributes without a dedicated painting UI.

A mask-preview color mode displays the final coverage in grayscale. It uses the ordinary color AOV and does not require a new public AOV. Returning to the shaded view restores the current effect/material binding.

Diagnostics identify the affected prim/subset and material, resolved setting sources, mask interpolation/count, wet-profile status, and the failed validation condition. Users must be able to distinguish an unprepared variant from an invalid mask or an unsupported base surface.

While a valid update is pending, keep a valid image/resource combination. On validation failure, retain the last valid effect only if its base binding and geometry revision still match; otherwise show the current dry material with an explicit effect error. Failed or pending wet requests must not be reported as successfully converged wet renders. Disabling the effect clears its failure and allows ordinary dry rendering.

items.title: Acceptance criteria
items.text:
Test Required result Dry identity Disabled/zero-amount bindings use the original material and original public parameter values Uniform coating Coverage 1 produces the intended water slab above the base; 0.5 is a stable partial-coverage result Mask domains Constant, uniform, vertex/varying, face-varying, and indexed inputs agree with their USD face/point domains Mask preview Values 0, 0.5, and 1, a ramp, and hard face boundaries appear in the correct places within the transport tolerance Shared materials Two prims sharing a base material retain independent wet amounts, roughness, and masks References and subsets Placement-prim overrides, renamed reference roots, instance expansion, subset edits/removal, and parent transforms preserve the intended result Base details Normal maps, metallic response, existing coat, and prepared UDIM tiles survive the added water slab Live edits Amount, roughness, and mask edits change a new delivered image without shader compilation; mask-only changes avoid geometry uploads Synchronization Stale geometry revisions are rejected; topology/resize/delete/recreate cases do not reuse incorrect mask buffers or material instances Path Tracer Zero new samples before all resources are ready; edits reset accumulation; a valid request reaches 64 samples and reports convergence Native comparison Generated native UE and Hydra renders use matched cameras, lights, time, seeds, and sample counts; the owned comparison fixture stays below 1% normalized RGB RMSE Failure and recovery Missing variants/masks, invalid data, wrong sessions/threads, and unsupported bases produce actionable errors; disable/fix/undo recovers Lifetime and privacy Repeated delegates keep one UE initialization; resources are released; source layers/files and publication rules are preserved

Record preparation/compile time, first ready frame, scalar-edit latency, mask upload bytes/time, frame time in both modes, shader closure/storage cost, and VRAM. Compare with the same dry scene on the same hardware. Performance claims require these measurements; the first release does not set a hardware-independent FPS target.

items.title: Implementation sequence
items.text:
1. Shader proof of concept: compose the water slab above an imported opaque base, verify coverage endpoints, retained base details, and closure/storage budgets in both renderers.
  2. Mask transport proof of concept: carry a procedural ramp through a dynamic mesh, verify linear values and face discontinuities, and exercise updates without topology uploads.
  3. Integration: add the cooked profile record, binding isolation, USD settings resolution, optional C ABI, revision tracking, and residency gating.
  4. Artist workflow and regression: add Solaris controls, mask preview, owned fixtures, reference/GeomSubset cases, recovery tests, and native comparisons.

Shader composition and mask transport are the first technical gates. If either gate fails its contract, revise this specification with the measured limitation before expanding the implementation. Dust, snow, image masks, native asset slots, and multiple ordered coatings follow the first wet-profile release.

items.title: Game effects (Niagara)
items.text:
hdUE renders UE's Niagara effects: fire, sparks, smoke, lightning, explosions, the effects games use. You make or buy them in UE's editor, cook them into hdUE's runtime, and place them on a prim. hdUE simulates each one to the frame you render, as Sequencer plays a Niagara track, so a husk sequence and the Solaris viewport show the effect at the same moment of its life.

Three effects from Epic's free Niagara Examples Pack at frame 48 (2 s), in Realtime:

items.title: Bringing effects into hdUE
items.text:
hdUE renders cooked UE assets, as it does cooked meshes and Blueprints (see cooked native assets). The hdUE Unreal Asset LOP cooks them for you from a UE project:

  1. Put the effects in a UE 5.8 project. For a Fab pack, use Add to project in the Epic Games Launcher; a pack made for an earlier UE version goes into a 5.8 project when you pick the closest version in Select Version.
  2. Add an hdUE Unreal Asset LOP (TAB menu > hdUE > Scene). Set UE Project to the project's .uproject and pick the effect in Asset: the menu lists the project's levels and the assets named with UE's prefixes (NS_ for Niagara Systems, SM_, SK_, BP_, SVT_).
  3. Press Import. UE's editor cooks the effect and what it uses in the background (about a minute for one effect) and adds it to the running hdUE runtime: no restart. Imported turns on, and the prim renders the effect.

Your project is not changed: its content is copied into hdUE's UE project (unreal/HdUEBackend/Content) to cook. Import needs UE's editor (editor_root in .local/paths.json), as hdUE's Substrate materials do.

For a whole project at once, scripts/Prepare-ProjectAssets.ps1 cooks everything into a new runtime (point Houdini at the runtime.json it writes). It stops on assets that fail to compile; demo levels and editor tools that come with a pack often do: delete them from unreal/HdUEBackend/Content (never from your project) and run it again with -SkipCopy.

items.title: Placing an effect
items.text:
HoudiniUSD

The hdUE Unreal Asset LOP places what it imports: set Translate, Rotate and Scale, and Effect Start Frame, the frame the effect starts at. Its prim is a small box hdUE replaces with the effect.

For a prim of your own, use a Render Geometry Settings LOP: on its Unreal Engine tab, set Native Asset to the effect (the menu lists the runtime's Niagara Systems with its other cooked assets) and Effect Start Frame.

def Mesh "fire"
{
    string primvars:unreal:asset = "/Game/NiagaraExamples/FX_Misc/NS_Fire.NS_Fire" (interpolation = "constant") # (1)!
    float primvars:unreal:effect:startFrame = 1 (interpolation = "constant") # (2)!
    point3f[] points = [(-0.1, 0, -0.1), (-0.1, 0, 0.1), (-0.1, 0.2, -0.1), (-0.1, 0.2, 0.1), (0.1, 0, -0.1), (0.1, 0, 0.1), (0.1, 0.2, -0.1), (0.1, 0.2, 0.1)]
    int[] faceVertexCounts = [4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4]
    int[] faceVertexIndices = [0, 2, 3, 1, 4, 5, 7, 6, 0, 1, 5, 4, 2, 6, 7, 3, 0, 4, 6, 2, 1, 3, 7, 5]
    double3 xformOp:translate = (0, 0, 0.6)
    uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
}
  1. The Niagara System's UE object path in the runtime project. The mesh is a placeholder: the effect renders in its place.
  2. The frame the effect starts at. Without it, it starts at frame 0.

The effect sits at the prim's pivot, in UE's own size: an effect authored in UE is the same size in a metre stage and in a centimetre stage.

items.title: Time
items.text:
The effect's age is the frame rendered minus Effect Start Frame, in seconds at the scene's frame rate. hdUE drives it as Sequencer does (MovieSceneNiagaraSystemTrackTemplate.cpp): the component runs alone (solo), its age is set from the scene's time, and it simulates in steps of one frame.

The same effect at four ages:

  • Before its start frame the effect has not started; at the start frame it has just begun.
  • Going to a later frame simulates forward from where it is. Going back restarts it and simulates up to that frame again, so scrubbing backwards over a long shot is slower than playing forwards.
  • The frame waits for the simulation: a render of frame 200 of an effect that starts at 1 first simulates 200 frames.
  • Effects move by whole frames: motion blur's sub-frames see the frame's state, so an effect is sharp where the rest of the frame is blurred, as with Sequencer's frame-locked playback.
  • A Velocity AOV makes hdUE render the frame before each frame first, which restarts the effects: each frame then simulates them from their start, slower on long shots.

Repeatability. Niagara picks new random numbers each time an effect starts, unless the effect asks for the same ones: in UE's editor, turn on Determinism in the Niagara System's properties (and on its emitters). Without it, rendering the same frame twice gives different flames, as it does in UE's Movie Render Queue.

items.title: Render modes
items.text:
Realtime Path Tracer Effect renders yes yes Lights the effect carries (Niagara light renderer) light the scene yes no

Measured on the scene above (samples/docs/effects.usda): in the Path Tracer the fire renders, but no longer lights the floor or the box.

items.title: Effects that need a game
items.text:
Some effects in game packs only start when gameplay tells them to: impacts, footsteps and pickups that wait for an event, effects that read a character's skeleton, or effects fed by Niagara Data Channels. Placed on a prim, they render nothing or only their first burst. Looping effects (fire, smoke, electricity, ambient sparks) and effects that start on their own work as they do in the editor.

Effects that burst once at their start (an explosion, a firework) are over a second or two later: set Effect Start Frame a few frames before the frame you want to see.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix The effect is not in the Native Asset menu The runtime does not have it yet Import it with an hdUE Unreal Asset LOP Nothing renders at the start frame At age 0 the effect has emitted nothing yet Render a later frame, or set Effect Start Frame earlier A frame looks different each time it renders The effect is not deterministic Turn on Determinism on the Niagara System in UE's editor The effect renders nothing at any frame It waits for a game event or data channel Use a looping effect, or one that starts on its own Prepare-ProjectAssets.ps1 or Import stops on Blueprint or Control Rig errors A pack's demo level, characters or editor tools need plugins hdUE's project leaves out Delete those assets from unreal/HdUEBackend/Content and run it again with -SkipCopy

items.title: Fog
items.text:
Fog fills the scene with UE's Exponential Height Fog: a haze that is densest at the ground and thins with height. Turn on Volumetric Fog and lights scatter into it, so beams and shadows show in the air.

A spot light through the fog of samples/docs/fog.usda, without and with Volumetric Fog.

items.title: Using fog in Solaris
items.text:
There are three ways to add fog. Use one height fog per scene: UE draws only one.

Workflow Where Use it when Render settings Fog tab of hdUE Render Settings the fog belongs to a render, not to the scene Height fog prim hdUE Height Fog LOP the fog travels with the scene, as a fog actor in a UE level Local fog volume hdUE Local Fog Volume LOP you need a patch of fog in one place: a valley, a doorway

From the render settings:

  1. On hdUE Render Settings, open the Fog tab.
  2. Turn on Exponential Height Fog.
  3. Set Fog Density, then turn on Volumetric Fog for lit fog.

From a prim: add hdUE Height Fog (TAB menu > hdUE > Visual Effects). It creates an UnrealExponentialHeightFog prim with the same properties as the Fog tab. Its controls start at Do Nothing: set each one you want to author. The prim's height in the world is the fog's height, so move it with its transform. A height fog prim replaces the render settings' fog, whose switch and values are then ignored. With several prims, the first visible one by path renders.

Outside Houdini, author the attributes on the render settings prim:

def RenderSettings "Settings"
{
    bool unreal:heightFog = 1
    float unreal:heightFog:FogDensity = 0.3
    bool unreal:heightFog:bEnableVolumetricFog = 1
}

Every property of UE's Exponential Height Fog component is an unreal:heightFog:<Property> attribute, with UE's name. Distances are in centimetres, as in UE's Details panel. The Fog reference lists them all with their defaults. This page covers the ones you change most.

All figures below use samples/docs/fog.usda: an 8 m closed room, a spot light at exposure 12 with a 15° cone, a sphere in the beam, Fog Density 0.3 and Volumetric Fog on. Realtime mode.

items.title: Exponential Height Fog
items.text:
Exponential Height Fog (unreal:heightFog) · Default Off

Places the fog in the scene, as an Exponential Height Fog actor does in a UE level. See Exponential Height Fog.

items.title: Fog Height
items.text:
Fog Height (unreal:heightFogHeight) · Default 0

The height of the fog actor, in scene units along the stage's up axis. The density is Fog Density at this height, grows below it and falls above it. A height fog prim uses its own position instead. See Fog Height.

items.title: Fog Density
items.text:
Fog Density (unreal:heightFog:FogDensity) · Default 0.02

How thick the fog is at the fog height. UE's slider goes to 0.05, which suits fog seen over hundreds of metres. A room needs more: the sample uses 0.3. See Fog Density.

items.title: Fog Height Falloff
items.text:
Fog Height Falloff (unreal:heightFog:FogHeightFalloff) · Default 0.2 · Range 0.001 to 2

How fast the density drops with height. Higher values keep the fog near the ground; lower values spread it over a taller band. Over a room's 4 m, only values near 2 show a gradient. See Fog Height Falloff.

A second fog layer, with its own density, falloff and height offset, is Second Fog Density, Second Fog Height Falloff and Second Fog Height Offset (unreal:heightFog:SecondFogData:*). Density 0, the default, turns it off.

items.title: Fog Inscattering Color
items.text:
Fog Inscattering Color (unreal:heightFog:FogInscatteringLuminance) · Default 0, 0, 0 · Realtime only

The light the fog itself adds, the same in every direction, as a luminance. With the default black, the fog only darkens what is behind it, unless Volumetric Fog lights it. Use it for distant haze that matches a sky. Within Volumetric Fog's View Distance, Volumetric Fog replaces it, as in UE. See Fog Inscattering Color.

Volumetric Fog off, so the inscattering colour shows on its own:

items.title: Volumetric Fog
items.text:
Volumetric Fog (unreal:heightFog:bEnableVolumetricFog) · Default Off

Lights the fog with the scene's lights and shadows: beams, light shafts and halos. Each light scatters into the fog by its Volumetric Scattering Intensity (unreal:light:VolumetricScatteringIntensity, default 1, on the Light LOP's Unreal Engine tab). Volumetric Fog ignores Start Distance, Fog Max Opacity and Fog Cutoff Distance. See Volumetric Fog.

Note

The Path Tracer renders the height fog only with Volumetric Fog on. Without it, a Path Tracer render shows no fog at all.

items.title: Scattering Distribution
items.text:
Scattering Distribution (unreal:heightFog:VolumetricFogScatteringDistribution) · Default 0.2 · Range -0.9 to 0.9

The phase function: where the fog sends the light it scatters. 0 scatters equally in all directions. Values toward 0.9 scatter forward, along the light's direction: a beam seen from the side fades, and a light facing the camera gets a bright halo. Keep it near 0 for beams seen from the side. See Scattering Distribution.

items.title: Albedo
items.text:
Albedo (unreal:heightFog:VolumetricFogAlbedo) · Default 1, 1, 1

The fog particles' reflectance. Water droplets are near white; dust is darker. A colour tints the scattered light. See Albedo.

items.title: Extinction Scale
items.text:
Extinction Scale (unreal:heightFog:VolumetricFogExtinctionScale) · Default 1 · Range 0.1 to 10

Scales how much light the fog particles absorb, without changing the density. Above 1, the fog absorbs more light everywhere. See Extinction Scale.

items.title: View Distance
items.text:
View Distance (unreal:heightFog:VolumetricFogDistance) · Default 6000 (60 m) · Range 1000 to 10000

How far from the camera Volumetric Fog is computed. Beyond it, the plain height fog takes over. Volumetric Fog has a fixed number of depth slices over this distance, so larger values reach further but sample each metre more coarsely. See View Distance.

items.title: Shadows in the fog
items.text:
Cast Volumetric Shadow (unreal:light:bCastVolumetricShadow, Light LOP > Unreal Engine tab) · Default Off (On for distant lights)

Lets the light's shadows cut through the fog. Without it, the sphere in the beam casts no shadow in the air. Turning it on costs GPU time per light. See Cast Volumetric Shadow.

items.title: Local fog volumes
items.text:
A Local Fog Volume is a sphere of fog that fades out toward its edge, combined with a height fog along its up axis. Use it for fog in one place: a valley, a pool of mist, smoke in a room.

  1. Add hdUE Local Fog Volume (TAB menu > hdUE > Visual Effects). It creates an UnrealLocalFogVolume prim.
  2. Place it with the transform section. Uniform Scale is the radius: at 1, the volume is UE's base sphere of 500 cm radius.
  3. Set Radial Fog Density and Height Fog Density (both 1 by default).

In Create mode the LOP authors every property, at UE's defaults too. Edit mode changes existing prims. The properties are listed in the USD prim reference.

Local fog volumes follow UE's rules:

  • They render in Realtime only. UE's Path Tracer ignores them.
  • UE draws none within 10 m of the camera (r.LocalFogVolume.GlobalStartDistance, which you can set as unreal:cvar:r:LocalFogVolume:GlobalStartDistance). A volume's own Start Distance can only push it further.
  • Height Fog Density 0 hides the whole volume: UE multiplies the radial and height coverages. For radial fog alone, use a small height density such as 0.01.
  • With Volumetric Fog on the height fog, local volumes are lit and shadowed through it too.

items.title: Breaking up the fog
items.text:
Height fog and Local Fog Volumes are smooth: UE gives neither a noise or texture input. In UE, uneven fog comes from fog particles: particles with a Volume-domain material add their own density to Volumetric Fog, and a noise in that material breaks it into wisps and gaps (Volumetric Fog in UE 5.8, "Local controls"). hdUE does the same with USD points: give a Points prim the primvars below, and each point becomes a sphere of fog, as wide as the point, in Volumetric Fog.

Primvar on the Points prim (constant) Type Default What it does primvars:unreal:fog:extinction float 0 Density at a sphere's centre, per metre. Above 0, the points render as fog instead of spheres primvars:unreal:fog:noiseStrength float 0 How much the noise breaks up the density: 0 is smooth, 1 leaves clear gaps and denser pockets primvars:unreal:fog:noiseSize float 1 m Size of the noise's pockets, in scene units primvars:unreal:fog:noiseOffset float3 (0, 0, 0) Moves the noise, in scene units: animate it for drifting fog primvars:unreal:fog:edgeSoftness float 1 How a sphere fades from its centre to its edge: higher fades sooner, for softer edges primvars:unreal:fog:albedo color3f (1, 1, 1) Fraction of the light the fog scatters primvars:unreal:fog:emissive color3f (0, 0, 0) Light the fog gives off, per unit of density
  1. Turn on Exponential Height Fog and Volumetric Fog: fog particles add to the volumetric fog, and nothing shows without it. A low Fog Density (0.02 to 0.05) leaves the particles to shape the fog.
  2. Scatter points where the fog should be (a Scatter SOP on the ground, for example) and give them a size with pscale. A SOP Import turns them into a Points prim and converts pscale into USD widths; hdUE reads widths as each sphere's diameter, so check it in the Scene Graph Details pane.
  3. Add the primvars with an Edit Properties LOP (or a wrangle) on the Points prim: at least primvars:unreal:fog:extinction, and primvars:unreal:fog:noiseStrength for uneven fog.

The fog room of samples/docs/fog.usda: 26 fog particles along the spot light's beam and where it lands, over a thin height fog (Realtime):

How it maps to UE:

  • Each point is a UE primitive with hdUE's M_HdUEFogParticle material: Volume domain, density fading from the point to its radius, times 3D gradient noise in world space, as UE's Volumetric Fog page builds its fog particles.
  • UE documents Volume-domain materials for particles. hdUE gives each point its own static mesh component instead, which UE voxelizes the same way: as a camera-facing quad over the primitive's bounding sphere (VolumetricFogVoxelization.cpp). One instanced mesh for all the points would give one sphere around them all.
  • Like the rest of Volumetric Fog, fog particles render in Realtime only, and Volumetric Fog's View Distance limits how far away they show.
  • A point's own material and displayColor are ignored while it is fog.

items.title: Recipes
items.text:
How to get light shafts in a dark room

  1. Exponential Height Fog: on.
  2. Fog Density: 0.3 (an 8 m room).
  3. Volumetric Fog: on.
  4. Scattering Distribution: 0.2.
  5. Light: a spot (SphereLight with Shaping), cone 15°, exposure 12.
  6. Light > Unreal Engine > Cast Volumetric Shadow: on, so objects in the beam cut it.

How to get a low ground mist

  1. Exponential Height Fog: on, Fog Height at the ground.
  2. Fog Density: 0.3.
  3. Fog Height Falloff: 2.
  4. Volumetric Fog: on, so the mist takes the scene's light.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No fog in a Path Tracer render The Path Tracer renders the height fog only through Volumetric Fog Turn on Volumetric Fog Fog is invisible in a room Fog Density 0.02 is made for distances of hundreds of metres Raise it to 0.1 to 1 Fog is black, or only darkens the image Volumetric Fog off and Fog Inscattering Color black Turn on Volumetric Fog, or set an inscattering colour Objects in a beam cast no shadow in the fog Cast Volumetric Shadow is off on local lights Turn it on on the light Beam invisible from the side Scattering Distribution near 0.9 sends the light forward Lower it toward 0 Render settings fog changes do nothing A height fog prim in the scene takes its place Edit the prim, or remove it A Local Fog Volume does not show It is within 10 m of the camera, its Height Fog Density is 0, or you render with the Path Tracer Move the camera back or lower r.LocalFogVolume.GlobalStartDistance; set a small Height Fog Density; use Realtime

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
