items.text: hdUE places UE's own Exponential Height Fog and Local Fog Volume components, with UE's properties and defaults; the Fog tab is generated from UE's source. UE's USD importer imports no fog, so there is no USD schema to follow. Karma has no height fog: in Karma you build fog as a volume.

items.title: Sky and clouds
items.text:
The sky is UE's Sky Atmosphere: a physical sky lit by your sun. Move the sun and the sky changes with it, from a blue midday sky to an orange sunset. UE's Volumetric Cloud adds a cloud layer on top.

The sun's elevation above the horizon, with Sky Atmosphere on and no dome light.

items.title: Using the sky in Solaris
items.text:
1. Remove or deactivate any DomeLight. A dome's environment takes the place of the sky's lighting.
  2. Add a Distant Light for the sun. Its rotation sets the sun's direction; its Atmosphere Sun Light (Unreal Engine tab) is on by default.
  3. On hdUE Render Settings, open the Sky tab and turn on Sky Atmosphere.
  4. For clouds, also turn on Volumetric Cloud on the same tab.

Without a DomeLight, hdUE adds a Sky Light that captures the sky in real time, as UE's default level has. The sky then lights the scene: Lumen needs it, and the Path Tracer renders the atmosphere through it.

Outside Houdini:

def RenderSettings "Settings"
{
    bool unreal:skyAtmosphere = 1
    bool unreal:volumetricCloud = 1
}

Every property of UE's Sky Atmosphere component is an unreal:skyAtmosphere:<Property> attribute, and every Volumetric Cloud property is unreal:volumetricCloud:<Property>, with UE's names. UE's atmosphere is measured in kilometres. The Sky reference lists them all with their defaults.

As scene prims. hdUE Sky Atmosphere and hdUE Volumetric Cloud (TAB menu > hdUE > Visual Effects) create UnrealSkyAtmosphere and UnrealVolumetricCloud prims with the same properties, as the actors are placed in a UE level. Their controls start at Do Nothing. A prim replaces its render settings counterpart; with several prims of a kind, the first visible one by path renders. See the USD prim reference.

The figures use samples/docs/lights.usda outdoors: its dome and key light off, the normalized sun (exposure 2) on, the camera level with the horizon. Realtime mode.

items.title: Sky Atmosphere
items.text:
Sky Atmosphere (unreal:skyAtmosphere) · Default Off

Places UE's Sky Atmosphere in the scene. Distant lights with Atmosphere Sun Light on light it and draw their sun disk in it. See Sky Atmosphere.

items.title: The sun
items.text:
The sky's colour comes from the sun's elevation: the lower the sun, the longer its light travels through the air and the redder it gets. Rotate the Distant Light to set the time of day.

Light property (Light LOP > Unreal Engine) Default What it does Atmosphere Sun Light (unreal:light:bAtmosphereSunLight) On The light lights the atmosphere and clouds and draws a sun disk Atmosphere Sun Light Index (unreal:light:AtmosphereSunLightIndex) 0 Two atmosphere lights: 0 for the sun, 1 for a moon or second sun Atmosphere Sun Disk Color Scale (unreal:light:AtmosphereSunDiskColorScale) 1, 1, 1 Multiplies the sun disk's colour Cast Cloud Shadows (unreal:light:bCastCloudShadows) Off Clouds shadow the atmosphere and the ground

The sun disk's size is the Distant Light's Angle (inputs:angle; 0.53° is the real sun). See the light properties reference.

items.title: Mie Scattering Scale
items.text:
Mie Scattering Scale (unreal:skyAtmosphere:MieScatteringScale) · Default 0.003996 · Range 0 to 5

Mie scattering comes from larger particles: dust, pollen, pollution. More of it makes the sky hazy and whiter and the halo around the sun larger. See Mie Scattering Scale.

Mie Anisotropy (unreal:skyAtmosphere:MieAnisotropy, default 0.8) sets how forward that light scatters: higher values concentrate the halo around the sun.

items.title: Rayleigh Scattering Scale
items.text:
Rayleigh Scattering Scale (unreal:skyAtmosphere:RayleighScatteringScale) · Default 0.0331 · Range 0 to 2

Rayleigh scattering comes from air molecules. It scatters blue more than red: it makes the sky blue by day and sunsets red. Raise it for a deeper blue sky; lower it for a paler one. See Rayleigh Scattering Scale.

items.title: Volumetric Cloud
items.text:
Volumetric Cloud (unreal:volumetricCloud) · Default Off

A layer of ray-marched clouds, lit by the sun and the sky. It needs Sky Atmosphere on. See Volumetric Cloud.

Parameter Default What it does Layer Bottom Altitude (unreal:volumetricCloud:LayerBottomAltitude) 5 km Height of the cloud base above the ground Layer Height (unreal:volumetricCloud:LayerHeight) 10 km Thickness of the cloud layer Material (unreal:volumetricCloud:Material) UE's m_SimpleVolumetricCloud_Inst The cloud material, as the path of a cooked material View Sample Count Scale (unreal:volumetricCloud:ViewSampleCountScale) 1 Ray-marching samples: higher is smoother and slower (Realtime only)

The cloud shapes come from the material. For other shapes or coverage, cook your own cloud material in UE and set Material to its path.

items.title: Path Tracer
items.text:
The Path Tracer renders the atmosphere through the Sky Light hdUE adds. For clouds, and for the atmosphere traced directly, turn on Reference Atmosphere (unreal:postProcess:PathTracingEnableReferenceAtmosphere, Rendering tab, default Off). With it on, UE ignores any Sky Light. See Reference Atmosphere.

Several art-direction properties render in Realtime only: Sky Luminance Factor, MultiScattering and the aerial perspective settings. The reference marks each one.

items.title: Recipes
items.text:
How to get a sunset

  1. Sky Atmosphere: on. No DomeLight.
  2. Distant Light: rotate X to -3 (the sun 3° above the horizon) and Y so the sun sits in front of the camera.
  3. Distant Light Angle: 0.53, Normalize on.
  4. Mie Scattering Scale: 0.01, for a warmer haze around the sun.
  5. Optional: Volumetric Cloud on, and Cast Cloud Shadows on the sun.

How to get an overcast day

  1. Sky Atmosphere and Volumetric Cloud: on. No DomeLight.
  2. Distant Light: rotate X to -50 (sun high), Cast Cloud Shadows on.
  3. Mie Scattering Scale: 0.05, for a white, hazy sky.
  4. Layer Bottom Altitude: 1 (km), for a low cloud base.
  5. The coverage is the cloud material's. For a closed cloud deck, set Material to a cooked cloud material with full coverage.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix The sky is black Sky Atmosphere is on but no Distant Light has Atmosphere Sun Light on Add a Distant Light, or turn its Atmosphere Sun Light on The sky shows but the scene keeps its old lighting A DomeLight is present: its environment lights the scene Deactivate the DomeLight No clouds Sky Atmosphere is off, or you render with the Path Tracer without Reference Atmosphere Turn on Sky Atmosphere; in the Path Tracer, turn on Reference Atmosphere Render settings sky changes do nothing An UnrealSkyAtmosphere or UnrealVolumetricCloud prim takes their place Edit the prim, or remove it

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text: hdUE places UE's Sky Atmosphere and Volumetric Cloud components with UE's properties and defaults, and lights them with distant lights as UE's directional lights do. Karma's sky is a separate Karma Sky Atmosphere LOP with its own parameters: values do not carry over.

items.title: Volumes
items.text:
A Volume prim, such as a VDB of smoke or a cloud, renders as a UE Heterogeneous Volume: fog with its own density field, lit and shadowed by the scene's lights. It renders in both Realtime and the Path Tracer.

The fog sphere of samples/cornell/variants/volume.usda in both render modes.

items.title: Using volumes in Solaris
items.text:
1. Bring the volume in with a Volume LOP (a .vdb file) or a SOP Import of a SOP volume.
  2. Make sure the Volume prim has a density field. hdUE renders that field, or the first field when none is named density.
  3. Render. The volume needs no material: hdUE's default volume material has an albedo of 0.8, and the density is the extinction per scene unit.

hdUE reads the field from:

  • an OpenVDBAsset that points to a .vdb file;
  • a SOP volume in the Solaris viewport, not yet saved to disk (an op: path on an OpenVDBAsset or HoudiniFieldAsset);
  • a .bgeo or .bgeo.sc file, which is where the USD Render ROP writes Houdini volumes for husk.

In a Houdini file, the VDB or Houdini volume primitive named by the field's fieldName is used, else the one at fieldIndex.

Outside Houdini:

def Volume "fog"
{
    rel field:density = </fog/density>
    def OpenVDBAsset "density"
    {
        asset filePath = @fog.vdb@
        token fieldName = "density"
    }
}

items.title: Breaking up a volume with noise
items.text:
Real mist, smoke and haze are never uniform. A box or sphere of constant density looks like a solid object: it has hard edges and the same brightness everywhere. Shape the density field itself with noise, in SOPs, before it reaches Solaris. The noise then renders the same in Realtime, the Path Tracer and Karma, because hdUE renders whatever field it is given.

  1. Volume SOP: name density, the size of the region, an initial value of the density you want at its thickest (3 here: extinction per metre).
  2. Volume Noise Fog SOP: Operation Multiply, Noise Type Sparse Convolution, Element Size about the size of the pockets you want (0.6 m here). Set the range so part of it falls below 0 (Min -1.2, Max 1.8 here) and clamp at 0: those parts become clear air, which breaks up the volume's outline.
  3. Convert VDB (VDB, fog class), then a SOP Import LOP, or write the VDB and load it with a Volume LOP.

The 4 x 3 m slab of samples/docs/mist.usda, lit by a low sun (Realtime). scripts/build_docs_volumes.py builds both volumes with these nodes:

For cloud shapes, the Cloud Noise SOP and its billowy and wispy variants do the same job on a cloud's density.

Unreal Engine's own fog has no noise input

UE's Exponential Height Fog and Local Fog Volumes are smooth by design: neither has a noise or texture input. In UE you break up fog with a heterogeneous volume (a VDB, as here) or with particles that use a Volume-domain material, which add density to Volumetric Fog. See Breaking up the fog.

items.title: Render modes
items.text:
Realtime Path Tracer Volume renders yes yes Shadows on the scene from distant lights, and from local lights with MegaLights off; the light needs Cast Volumetric Shadow yes, from every light, with multiple scattering Emission yes yes

In Realtime, shadows are UE's heterogeneous volume shadow casting. UE's MegaLights does not support heterogeneous volumes, so a local light shaded by MegaLights casts no volume shadow: turn off MegaLights (unreal:megaLights, Light LOP > Unreal Engine tab) on that light. Cast Volumetric Shadow (unreal:light:bCastVolumetricShadow, Light LOP > Unreal Engine tab) is on by default for distant lights and off for the others. See Cast Volumetric Shadow.

The Path Tracer re-voxelizes the volumes for each frame. Batch renders (husk) use the shading rate and memory UE's documentation recommends for cinematic renders, so silhouettes stay sharp.

items.title: Emission
items.text:
A volume emits light from a second field, such as temperature or flame, when you name it. The emitted colour is UE's BlackBody of the field's value, in kelvin.

Primvar on the Volume prim Default What it does primvars:unreal:emissionField none The field that emits. Without it nothing emits primvars:unreal:temperatureScale 1 Kelvin per unit of the field's value primvars:unreal:emissionIntensity 1 Multiplies the emitted light

These are constant primvars: in Houdini, detail attributes on the volume become them. The emission field is sampled at the density field's voxels; outside its own grid it reads 0.

The Cornell fog sphere emitting from its own density field, at a Temperature Scale of 2500 (Path Tracer):

As in UE, nothing emits unless you ask: UE's heterogeneous volumes emit what their material makes of a grid, and prescribe no field.

items.title: Materials
items.text: Without a material, volumes render with hdUE's default volume material. In Houdini's viewport, a bound Substrate Builder volume material replaces it; see Substrate Builder. Other volume materials are not translated.

items.title: Sparse Volume Textures
items.text: A VDB imported into a UE project as a Sparse Volume Texture renders through the Native Asset field (Render Geometry Settings LOP > Unreal Engine tab), as a UE Heterogeneous Volume, in both modes. UE reads the VDB's units as centimetres, so a VDB written in metres needs a scale of 100 on the prim. For an animated sequence, Volume Frame (primvars:unreal:volume:frame) picks the frame, from 0 for the first file: set it to $F - 1 for a sequence starting at frame 1. See cooked native assets.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix The volume does not render The Volume prim has no field hdUE reads, or its file is missing Name the density field density; check the file path No volume shadow in Realtime The light is a local light shaded by MegaLights, or its Cast Volumetric Shadow is off Turn off MegaLights on the light, turn on Cast Volumetric Shadow, or use a distant light Volume looks blocky Grids larger than 512 voxels on an axis are point-sampled with a stride Render with the Path Tracer for detail, or resample the VDB to 512 voxels per axis A tapered (frustum) VDB renders wrong Frustum VDBs and tapered Houdini volumes are not translated Resample to a regular grid The volume does not glow No primvars:unreal:emissionField Name the emitting field, then tune Temperature Scale

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text: hdUE renders volumes with UE's Heterogeneous Volumes, as UE does for a VDB placed in a level. Compared with Karma on the Cornell fog sphere, a Realtime fog's brightness is within about 15%. The Path Tracer's shadow is lighter than Karma's: an optical depth of 1.4 against Karma's 1.9.

items.title: Displacement
items.text:
Displacement moves a surface along its normals by a height from the material, so bumps become real geometry: they cast shadows and change the silhouette. hdUE dices and displaces the mesh before UE renders it, so Lumen, the Path Tracer and Nanite all see the same surface.

A flat plate displaced by a 128 x 128 bump texture, at three heights (Path Tracer).

items.title: Using displacement in Solaris
items.text:
1. Connect a height to the material's displacement:
    • UsdPreviewSurface: its Displacement input (inputs:displacement), a distance in the mesh's units.
    • MaterialX: an ND_displacement_float node on the material's displacement output. The height is its displacement times its scale.
  2. For a texture, read it with a UsdUVTexture (or MaterialX image) through the mesh's UVs. Its Scale sets the height: the sample's texture at scale 0.6 raises the white bumps 0.6 m.
  3. Render. There is no setting to turn on: every mesh whose material displaces is displaced.

items.title: How the mesh is diced
items.text:
A flat mesh has too few points to show a texture's detail. Before displacing, hdUE splits every triangle into 4, as many times as needed:

  • It dices until the mesh has about one triangle per two texels of the displacement texture.
  • It stops at about one million triangles per mesh.
  • A constant displacement (no texture) moves the points without dicing.

The sample's plate is one quad (2 triangles). Its 128 x 128 texture has 16,384 texels, so the plate is diced 6 times, into 8,192 triangles.

After displacing, normals are recomputed from the displaced surface. A UV seam stays closed where the texture is the same on both sides. Hard edges (split normals) open into cracks, because each side moves along its own normal.

The dicing is uniform over the mesh, not adaptive to the camera: a mesh far from the camera is diced as finely as one near it. A subdivision mesh is first refined to its Subdivision Level, then diced.

items.title: Recipes
items.text:
How to get sharp displacement detail

  1. Use a displacement texture at the resolution the detail needs: a 1024 x 1024 map dices to about 500,000 triangles; 2048 x 2048 and larger reach the one-million-triangle limit.
  2. Split a large displaced surface into several meshes: the limit is per mesh.
  3. Keep the texture's colour space raw, so the heights are linear.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No displacement; the log warns "cannot displace with ..." The texture cannot be read, or the mesh lacks the UVs it reads Fix the path; add the UV primvar the texture reads Displacement is soft or stair-stepped A small texture limits dicing, or the mesh reached the one-million-triangle limit Use a larger texture; split the mesh Cracks open along edges Hard edges (split normals) move apart Use smooth normals across the edge, or a subdivision mesh A MaterialX vector displacement does nothing Only float displacement (ND_displacement_float) is translated; a warning names it Convert to a float height A wet surface is not displaced Meshes with wet surface effects keep their points Remove the wet surface from that mesh

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text: UE's own displacement, Nanite tessellation and World Position Offset, is not used: UE 5.8's ray-traced geometry ignores both, and the Path Tracer renders that geometry, so it would not see them. Dicing the mesh gives every mode the same surface. Karma dices adaptively, by the size of the surface on screen; hdUE dices uniformly by the texture's resolution.

items.title: Hair
items.text:
hdUE renders curves as UE hair strands: the strands UE's groom system draws, with UE's hair shading, in Realtime and in the Path Tracer. Without it, curves render as thin tubes.

12,000 strands on a 25 cm head, under one rect light: Hair Strands off, the curves as tubes; on, UE hair strands. Drag to compare.

items.title: Rendering curves as hair
items.text:
HoudiniUSD
  1. Bring the curves into Solaris: a groom from the Hair Generate SOP, or any curves, through a SOP Import LOP. Give them a width: Houdini's width (or pscale) point attribute becomes USD's widths. Real hair is 0.05 to 0.1 mm thick; widths of 0.2 to 0.6 mm read well at a few metres.
  2. Add a Render Geometry Settings LOP and select the curves, or a prim above them.
  3. On its Unreal Engine tab, turn on Hair Strands.
def BasisCurves "hair"
{
    uniform token type = "linear"
    int[] curveVertexCounts = [16, 16, ...]
    point3f[] points = [...]
    float[] widths = [...] (interpolation = "vertex") # (1)!
    bool primvars:unreal:groom = 1 (interpolation = "constant") # (2)!
}
  1. Per point, tapering from root to tip; one constant width works too.
  2. On the curves or an ancestor: a primvar is inherited.

hdUE builds the UE groom asset UE's importer would make from a groom file, with UE's own groom builder, from the curves' evaluated points and widths: one group, guides from every strand, no simulation. Linear and cubic curves (Bezier, B-spline, Catmull-Rom) are both evaluated to points first.

items.title: Colour and materials
items.text:
The same groom with UE's default hair material, a groom_color per strand, and a bound Substrate Builder Substrate Hair material. Drag to compare.

The strands take their look from, in this order:

  1. A bound UE hair material: a Substrate Builder material whose graph has a Substrate Hair node, prepared as any Substrate Builder material. MaterialX's chiang_hair_bsdf goes through UE's MaterialX importer the same way.
  2. The groom's own colour and roughness: the groom_color and groom_roughness primvars, which hdUE's hair material reads through UE's Hair Attributes node, as a UE hair material does. Without groom_color and without a bound material, displayColor gives the colour, as it does for unbound meshes. In Houdini, name the attributes groom_color and groom_roughness (or set Cd), per point or per curve.
  3. A bound Preview Surface or Standard Surface: its base colour and roughness, as constants (textures are not read).
  4. Otherwise, UE's default hair material.

items.title: Groom attributes
items.text:
Every groom_* primvar on the curves reaches the UE groom, under the names UE's groom importers use, so a UE hair material reads it with Hair Attributes:

Primvar Type UE groom_color color3f, per point or per curve Hair Attributes > Base Color groom_roughness float, per point or per curve Hair Attributes > Roughness groom_ao float, per point or per curve Hair Attributes > AO groom_root_uv float2, per curve Hair Attributes > Root UV groom_clumpid int, per curve Hair Attributes > Clump ID groom_id int, per curve the strand's ID

As in UE's USD importer, uniform and constant primvars are per curve and vertex or varying ones per point. UE reads colour, roughness and AO per point only: hdUE spreads a per-curve value over its curve's points.

items.title: Instancing
items.text: Curves under a PointInstancer render as one groom built once and drawn once per instance, as instanced meshes are. A shear in an instance's transform is dropped (UE's components hold none).

items.title: Realtime and Path Tracer
items.text:
The same groom in Realtime (Lumen) and in UE's Path Tracer, which traces the strands' geometry. Drag to compare.

In Realtime, UE draws hair with its own strand rasterizer and hair shading model; depth of field can use the hair's own depth with Use Hair Depth (unreal:postProcess:DepthOfFieldUseHairDepth, hdUE Render Settings > Lens > Depth of Field).

items.title: Not yet translated
items.text:
• Simulation: UE's hair physics does not run; the strands render where the curves are.
  • Textures on a bound Preview Surface or Standard Surface: its constant colour and roughness are used.
  • MaterialX chiang_hair_bsdf renders black: UE's own translation of it (MX_ChiangHairBSDF) draws the strands black, with or without absorption. Use a Substrate Hair material instead.

For hair cards (textured polygon strips), use a mesh with the Substrate Builder's Substrate Hair node.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Curves render as tubes, not hair Hair Strands is off Turn it on on the curves or an ancestor The hair looks like straw or a solid sheet No widths (hdUE then uses 0.01 scene units: 1 cm strands in a metre scene), or widths in the wrong unit Author widths in scene units: 0.0002 to 0.0006 in a metre scene The hair stays UE's default colour No groom_color, displayColor or bound material, or the bound material is not a hair material Add groom_color, or bind a Substrate Hair material A bound material renders as UE's default hair The material has no Substrate Hair node, so UE cannot draw strands with it (a warning names it) Use a Substrate Hair material, or let groom_color colour the strands MaterialX hair is black UE's translation of chiang_hair_bsdf Use a Substrate Hair material

items.title: Geometry
items.text:
hdUE renders the geometry of your USD stage as UE geometry: meshes, curves and hair, points, instancers and implicit shapes. This page says what each prim type becomes in UE and which USD attributes it reads.

USD prim Renders in UE as Mesh a static mesh, Nanite where it can be (Nanite) Mesh with catmullClark or loop scheme a refined mesh at the subdivision level Cube, Sphere, Cone, Cylinder, Capsule, Plane a mesh BasisCurves tubes, or UE hair strands NurbsCurves, NurbsPatch the evaluated curve or surface Points one sphere per point PointInstancer, instanceable references instanced static meshes Volume a UE Heterogeneous Volume (Volumes) HermiteCurves not rendered; a warning names the prim

items.title: Meshes
items.text:
Meshes keep their points, face-varying UVs, normals and colours. A mesh hdUE cannot convert (broken indices, or more than about 715 million vertices) is skipped with a warning naming it in the UE log; the rest of the scene renders.

Normals. Authored normals are kept (primvars:normals wins over normals). Missing normals are generated smooth, so faces that share a point share its normal. For hard edges, author face-varying normals or split the points. Subdivision meshes ignore authored normals, as USD specifies.

Materials on faces. A GeomSubset of family materialBind binds a material to some faces. Faces in no subset keep the mesh's material. Overlapping or invalid subsets are rejected.

Holes, orientation, concave polygons. holeIndices, orientation = "leftHanded" and concave n-gons render as authored.

items.title: Double-sided meshes
items.text:
Cull Backface (unreal:cullBackface) · Default On

A mesh with doubleSided = false (USD's default) renders its front faces only, as UE's USD importer imports it. A mesh with doubleSided = true renders both sides, each lit as a front face. To render every mesh on both sides, as Karma does, turn Cull Backface off (hdUE Render Settings > Rendering tab, Show: Advanced). See Cull Backface.

Tip

A plane, a leaf or a single wall that vanishes from one side is single-sided. Author doubleSided = true on the mesh, or turn off Cull Backface.

Karma's per-object karma:object:cull_backface is not read: doubleSided is the per-mesh switch.

items.title: Implicit shapes
items.text: Cube, Sphere, Cone, Cylinder, Capsule and Plane prims, including the Cylinder_1 and Capsule_1 forms with separate top and bottom radii, are converted to meshes by Hydra. Hydra's sphere is a coarse Catmull-Clark cage, so it looks faceted at Subdivision Level 0: set it to 2 or more for round spheres.

items.title: Curves
items.text:
BasisCurves render as six-sided tubes, with flat caps on open curves.

  • Linear curves follow their points. Cubic Bezier, B-spline and Catmull-Rom curves follow their basis. Periodic curves close.
  • widths sets the diameter, per curve or per point. Unauthored, the width is 0.01.
  • displayColor per point or per curve colours them when no material is bound.

items.title: Hair
items.text: Curves render as UE hair strands when you turn on Hair Strands (primvars:unreal:groom) on them or an ancestor. See Hair.

items.title: Points
items.text: Points render as one sphere per point, sized by widths (the diameter; 0.1 when unauthored). Per-point displayColor colours them. Points with primvars:unreal:fog:extinction render as fog instead: see Breaking up the fog.

items.title: Instancing
items.text:
PointInstancers, nested PointInstancers and instanceable references (USD native instancing) render as UE instanced static meshes: each prototype is built once and drawn once per instance.

PointInstancer attribute Read protoIndices, positions, orientations, orientationsf, scales yes invisibleIds, inactiveIds yes: those instances are not drawn velocities, accelerations, angularVelocities yes, for motion blur instance-rate primvars, such as displayColor yes: each instance gets its colour

Points, curves and volumes under an instancer are drawn once per instance too.

UE instances cannot shear. An instance whose transform shears (a rotated prototype under a non-uniform scale) renders as a separate mesh with its points transformed; the others stay UE instances. A prototype that is a cooked UE mesh (Native Asset) cannot be transformed that way, so its sheared instances render without shear, with a warning.

items.title: Primvars
items.text:
UVs. A mesh's UVs come from the primvar its material's texture reads (the varname of a UsdPrimvarReader, such as st, or map1 from a 3ds Max export), else from st. A mesh carries up to four UV sets, one per primvar its material reads.

Display colour. Geometry with no material renders with a Preview Surface (roughness 0.5) whose base colour is displayColor, as UE's USD importer draws unbound prims. A prim with no displayColor renders white, as in UE's importer. A displayColor that varies (per face, point, vertex, curve or instance) is applied as vertex or instance colours. Mesh vertex colours are stored in 8 bits, so very dark colours band slightly.

Not translated: varying displayOpacity, and colours on meshes that also carry a wet surface mask.

items.title: Visibility and purpose
items.text:
• visibility = "invisible" hides a prim and its children.
  • Purpose. Final renders include the purposes listed in the render settings prim's includedPurposes, by default default and render. Proxy and guide geometry does not render.
  • renderVisibility and guideVisibility (UsdGeomVisibilityAPI) are followed.
  • A model:drawMode of bounds or cards replaces the model with its box or cards, as UE's USD importer does.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix A wall or plane disappears from one side The mesh is single-sided Set doubleSided, or turn off Cull Backface Small points (dust, sparks, rain) show in the Path Tracer but vanish in Realtime Each point is smaller than a pixel: the Path Tracer adds its exact share of the pixel over many samples, while Realtime draws it on one sample per frame and temporal anti-aliasing (TSR) averages it away Make the points about a pixel wide at their distance, or render the shot with the Path Tracer A prim is missing; the UE log names it The mesh has broken indices or is too large Fix or split the mesh Hard edges look smooth No authored normals: hdUE generates smooth ones Author face-varying normals, or split the points Unbound geometry is white, not grey as in Karma No displayColor: hdUE uses white, as UE's importer does Author displayColor, or bind a material Proxy geometry renders, or render geometry is missing The render settings prim's includedPurposes Set includedPurposes to default and render Curves render as tubes, not hair Hair Strands is off Turn it on on the curves or an ancestor

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text: hdUE follows UE's USD importer: single-sided meshes are culled, unbound prims are white with their display colour, and draw modes apply. Karma renders both sides of every mesh by default and draws unbound prims grey. Turn off Cull Backface to match Karma's double-sided default.

items.title: Nanite
items.text:
Nanite is UE's virtualized geometry: it draws each mesh with about as many triangles as the image has pixels, whatever the mesh's own count. hdUE turns the static meshes of your stage into Nanite meshes, so scenes of hundreds of millions of triangles render in Realtime.

SideFX's shader ball lit, then in UE's Nanite views: each colour is one triangle, then one cluster of triangles.

items.title: When hdUE uses Nanite
items.text:
hdUE decides as UE's USD Stage Actor does: a mesh with at least Nanite Triangle Threshold triangles (unreal:naniteTriangleThreshold, default 1,000,000, UE's default) builds Nanite data; a smaller one stays a regular static mesh. Instancer prototypes always build Nanite: without it, every instance of a scattered prototype draws all its triangles.

Mesh Nanite Static meshes from your stage, at or above the threshold yes Static meshes below the threshold no, as in UE's USD import Instancer prototypes (PointInstancer, native instancing) yes Cooked UE meshes (Native Asset) with Nanite data yes Meshes with a translucent material no, as in UE Animated or edited meshes (deforming points, in the viewport while you edit) no: they stay regular meshes Meshes with a wet surface no

Identical meshes share one Nanite mesh, as UE's USD importer shares one asset between identical prims.

Batch renders (husk, the USD Render ROP) build all Nanite data before the first frame.

Houdini's viewport draws regular meshes first, builds Nanite data in the background, then swaps each mesh, one per frame. The viewport keeps drawing meanwhile and settles once the last mesh is in. On large scenes some meshes appear only when their build is swapped in: hdUE draws the regular meshes first only while they fit in 2 GB of GPU memory.

items.title: Nanite settings
items.text:
These are UE console variables, on hdUE Render Settings > Engine Quality tab (Show: Advanced).

Parameter Default What it does Nanite (unreal:cvar:r:Nanite) On Draws Nanite meshes with Nanite. Off, UE draws their fallback meshes Max Pixels per Edge (unreal:cvar:r:Nanite:MaxPixelsPerEdge) 1 The triangle edge length Nanite aims for, in pixels (Realtime only) Nanite Ray Tracing (unreal:cvar:r:RayTracing:Nanite:Mode) Fallback Mesh (0) What ray tracing sees: the fallback mesh (0) or the full Nanite geometry streamed for the view (1) Require Nanite (unreal:requireNanite) Off Cooked native meshes must render with Nanite

items.title: Max Pixels per Edge
items.text:
Max Pixels per Edge (unreal:cvar:r:Nanite:MaxPixelsPerEdge) · Default 1 · Range 0.25 to 8

Higher values draw fewer, larger triangles: faster, with coarser silhouettes. The Path Tracer does not use it.

items.title: Ray tracing and fallback meshes
items.text:
Nanite draws the rasterized image. Ray tracing (Lumen's reflections and the Path Tracer) traces each Nanite mesh's fallback mesh instead: a simplified copy UE's Nanite builder makes, at UE's default error (Fallback Target Auto). On most meshes the difference does not show. On thin geometry, such as foliage, the fallback is thinner and sparser in the Path Tracer and in Lumen's reflections.

Set Nanite Ray Tracing to 1 to trace the full Nanite geometry streamed for the view. It costs time: Intel Sponza's tree took 65 s instead of 25 s for a 256-sample husk frame, load included.

items.title: Cost and memory
items.text:
Building Nanite data is most of a scene's load time. hdUE caches each build on disk, as UE's derived data cache does for its static meshes:

  • The cache is %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\Saved\NaniteCache, or Saved/NaniteCache under HDUE_USER_DIR when it is set.
  • A cache entry not used for a week is removed.
  • 450 meshes of 9,800 triangles: 10.5 s to build, 0.7 s from the cache (75 MB on disk).
  • NVIDIA's Da Vinci Workshop (617 million triangles, 6,750 meshes): 11 minutes in husk with an empty cache (3.6 GB written), 2 minutes from it, with a peak of 22 GB of memory.

On the GPU, each Nanite mesh keeps one root page resident; the rest stream in from system memory when the view needs them, into UE's 512 MB streaming pool (r.Nanite.Streaming.StreamingPoolSize). When a view needs more than the pool holds, Nanite draws coarser clusters, as UE does. The root pages share one GPU buffer of at most 2 GB on NVIDIA (4 GB on AMD), less the streaming pool: tens of thousands of meshes. Near that limit, hdUE renders the remaining meshes as regular static meshes and writes a warning to the UE log.

In Houdini's viewport, background builds start only while their memory fits. The console variable r.HdUE.MeshBuildMaxMemoryUsage (in GB, default 0: all available memory) caps them lower; author it as int unreal:cvar:r:HdUE:MeshBuildMaxMemoryUsage on the render settings. In a Windows job with a memory limit, such as a farm container, the job's limit counts as the available memory.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Symptom Cause Fix First husk frame takes minutes Nanite data is being built; the cache is empty Render again: later renders read the cache. Keep Saved/NaniteCache on the farm, or point HDUE_USER_DIR at a shared disk Meshes pop in one by one in the viewport Nanite builds are swapped in as they finish Wait for the viewport to settle A mesh looks faceted in the Path Tracer but smooth in Realtime The mesh is Nanite (at or above Nanite Triangle Threshold, or an instancer prototype), and ray tracing sees its fallback mesh Raise Nanite Triangle Threshold above the mesh's triangle count Foliage looks thinner in the Path Tracer than in Realtime Ray tracing sees the fallback mesh of an instanced or very dense mesh Set Nanite Ray Tracing to 1 (its normals can show faint streaks in glossy reflections) Some meshes render without Nanite on a huge scene; the UE log warns The root page buffer is nearly full Merge small distinct meshes: each distinct mesh keeps a root page, while identical meshes share one Distant detail looks soft on a huge scene The view's geometry overflows the streaming pool, so Nanite draws coarser clusters Render at a lower resolution, or reduce unique geometry A translucent mesh is not in the Nanite views Translucent materials do not use Nanite, as in UE Expected Viewport runs out of memory while loading Too many background builds at once Set unreal:cvar:r:HdUE:MeshBuildMaxMemoryUsage to a few GB

To check which meshes are Nanite, set Debug View (unreal:debugView) to Nanite: Mask: see Debug views.

To render without Nanite, for comparison, set the environment variable HDUE_NANITE=0 before starting Houdini or husk.

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text: hdUE builds Nanite meshes with UE's own Nanite builder and settings, as UE's static mesh build does, for the meshes UE's USD Stage Actor would make Nanite, and ray traces their fallback meshes as UE does by default. One departure: instancer prototypes are Nanite at any size. Karma has no Nanite: it renders every triangle of the mesh.

items.title: Subdivision surfaces
items.text:
A subdivision mesh is a coarse control cage that renders as a smooth surface. hdUE refines Catmull-Clark and Loop meshes with OpenSubdiv to the level you set, keeping their creases, corners and holes.

A Catmull-Clark cube at levels 0 to 3 (Realtime).

items.title: Using subdivision in Solaris
Subdivision Level
items.text:
Subdivision Level (unreal:subdivisionLevel) · Default 0 · Range 0 to 5

How many times each subdivision mesh is refined. Each level multiplies the face count by 4: a 6-face cube has 384 faces at level 3. At 0, the default, meshes render as their control cage. See Subdivision Level.

Level Faces per cage face Looks like 0 (default) 1 the control cage 1 4 rounded but faceted 2 16 facets visible on close silhouettes 3 64 close to Karma's smooth surface on a cube

Implicit spheres (a USD Sphere prim) are meshed coarsely, so they look faceted at level 0.

items.title: Per-prim Subdivision Level
items.text:
Subdivision Level (primvars:unreal:subdivisionLevel, Render Geometry Settings LOP > Unreal Engine tab) · Default: the render setting

Replaces the render setting for the meshes of this prim. It is a constant primvar, so it can sit on an ancestor and reach every mesh below it. Use it to refine a hero mesh more than the background, or to keep a dense mesh at 0.

items.title: What follows the refined surface
items.text:
• Creases, corners and holes (creaseIndices, cornerIndices, holeIndices), and the boundary and face-varying interpolation rules.
  • Every primvar: UVs (st), displayColor, velocities and time-sampled points, of any interpolation.
  • GeomSubsets: a material bound to some faces stays on their refined faces.

Authored normals are ignored, as the USD specification says for subdivision surfaces. The refined vertices lie on the limit surface and take its exact normals (OpenSubdiv's limit evaluation), as Storm and Karma render it; UE's USD importer stops at the refined cage, whose normals show faint bands along the coarse faces in glossy reflections. Refinement is uniform; there is no adaptive or screen-space refinement. A displaced subdivision mesh is refined first, then diced further for its displacement: see Displacement.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix A smooth model renders blocky Subdivision Level is 0, UE's default Set it to 2 or 3 Hard edges are smoothed away Normals authored for hard edges are ignored on subdivision meshes Author creases, or set the mesh's scheme to none Memory and load time grow fast Each level has 4 times the faces of the one before Raise the level only on the meshes that need it, with the per-prim primvar A wet surface mask is missing on a subdivided mesh Wet surface masks are not translated on subdivided meshes Set the mesh's level to 0

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text: The default level 0 is UE's: UE's USD Stage Actor's Subdivision Level defaults to 0 and is the only, global, level. The per-prim primvar is hdUE's own. Karma refines subdivision surfaces by default, so a scene made for Karma needs about level 3 to match.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text: Most installs need no variable set by hand: Install.cmd writes a Houdini package file that sets the ones hdUE needs. The others are switches for troubleshooting and performance tests. Set them before you start Houdini or husk; they are read once per process.

items.title: What each one is for
items.text: You want to Use Run hdUE at all HDUE_RUNTIME_CONFIG, HDUE_HOUDINI_ENABLE (set by the package) Keep Unreal Engine's logs and Nanite cache on another drive HDUE_USER_DIR (default %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE) See where a frame's time goes HDUE_TRACE_TIMING, HDUE_TRACE_FILE Check what reaches Unreal Engine HDUE_TRACE_SETTINGS, HDUE_TRACE_SCENE, HDUE_TRACE_PASS Rule out a viewport or Nanite problem HDUE_GPU_FRAMES=0, HDUE_NANITE=0 Pass arguments to Unreal Engine HDUE_UE_ARGS

items.title: Variables
items.text:
The package file sets HDUE_RUNTIME_CONFIG and HDUE_HOUDINI_ENABLE (and HDUE, HDUE_VERSION); the rest are for development and debugging.

Variable Description HDUE_RUNTIME_CONFIG Runtime profile (backend_dll, runtime_project) the delegate starts UE from HDUE_HOUDINI_ENABLE 1 lets hdUE's Python host start in Houdini's UI when a viewer selects hdUE HDUE_BACKEND_DLL Backend DLL, overriding the runtime profile HDUE_HOUDINI_LOG_DIR Where the Houdini host writes its logs and state HDUE_NANITE 0 builds regular static meshes instead of Nanite HDUE_USER_DIR Where UE writes its logs and Nanite cache (default %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE) HDUE_GPU_FRAMES 0 reads Houdini viewport frames back to the CPU instead of sharing GPU textures HDUE_TRACE_PASS 1 prints one line per render pass to stderr HDUE_TRACE_SETTINGS 1 prints every render setting the delegate receives HDUE_TRACE_SCENE 1 prints scene submissions

The package file also sets:

Variable Description HDUE The package folder. Use it in paths: $HDUE/samples/cornell/cornell.usda HDUE_VERSION The package's hdUE version

These are read too, and not set by the package:

Variable Description HDUE_TRACE_TIMING 1 prints each frame's timeline: request to frame, readback, setting changes, scene uploads HDUE_TRACE_FILE File that receives the HDUE_TRACE_TIMING output instead of the console. Houdini's UI shows no console output, so set it there HDUE_UE_ARGS Arguments appended to Unreal Engine's command line. -stdout echoes every UE log line to the console HDUE_SHOW_WINDOW 1 opens Unreal Engine's window; by default it renders offscreen HDUE_VIRTUAL_TEXTURE_CACHE Folder for the UDIM virtual texture cache, instead of %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\VirtualTextureCache

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Trace the timeline of a husk render:

$env:HDUE_TRACE_TIMING = '1'
husk --renderer "Unreal Engine" -f 1 -n 4 -o render.$F4.exr scene.usd

Trace the viewport in Houdini, to a file:

$env:HDUE_TRACE_TIMING = '1'
$env:HDUE_TRACE_FILE = "$env:TEMP\hdue-trace.txt"
houdini

Record a GPU profile of 600 frames with Unreal Engine's CSV profiler (written to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\Saved\Profiling):

$env:HDUE_UE_ARGS = '-csvGpuStats -csvCaptureFrames=600'

Unreal Engine's own log is in %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\Saved\Logs (Saved\Logs under HDUE_USER_DIR when it is set; Unreal > Open Unreal Engine Logs in Houdini). Its timestamps are in UTC.

items.title: Your first render
items.text:
You will render the Cornell box with Unreal Engine: first in the Solaris viewport, then to an EXR on disk with husk. It takes about ten minutes once hdUE is installed.

The result, in Unreal Engine's two render modes:

items.title: The starting scene
items.text:
The package ships the Cornell box in $HDUE/samples/cornell/cornell.usda. It holds a camera, one rect light and a render settings prim set to the Path Tracer at 512 samples, 512 x 512 pixels.

  1. In a new Houdini session, go to the /stage network.
  2. Add a Sublayer LOP. Set File to $HDUE/samples/cornell/cornell.usda.
  3. Set its display flag.

A Sublayer LOP with no input copies the file's metadata to the stage, so the scene keeps its Z-up axis and metre units.

items.title: Render in the viewport
items.text:
1. In the Scene Viewer's renderer menu, pick Unreal Engine. The first time in a session, Unreal Engine starts inside Houdini. The image appears a few seconds later; later switches are immediate.
  2. In the viewport's camera menu, pick camera to look through the Cornell camera.
  3. Choose Unreal > Create hdUE Render Settings from the main menu bar. This adds an hdUE Render Settings LOP after the Sublayer and displays it. It takes the camera, the render mode and the sample count from the scene's own render settings.

The viewport now renders with the Path Tracer and refines the image up to 512 samples. While you tumble, scrub or play, it uses 8 samples per pixel, then refines again once the view is still.

The Cornell box through camera, after 512 Path Tracer samples.

items.title: Switch to Realtime
items.text:
On the hdUE Render Settings LOP, set Render Mode (unreal:renderMode) to Realtime (Lumen).

The same view in Realtime, after Lumen's 64 warmup frames.

Realtime is Unreal Engine's deferred renderer with Lumen global illumination and reflections, the renderer of a game or a Movie Render Queue shot. It is meant for final frames too. The Path Tracer is UE's reference renderer: it traces up to 32 bounces and takes about 50 times longer on this scene.

In Realtime, a still frame counts as finished after Warmup Frames (unreal:warmupFrames, default 64), the frames Lumen needs to gather its lighting. You can also switch with Unreal > Render Mode > Realtime or Path Traced.

items.title: Turn on the Unreal Tonemapper
items.text:
The Cornell box renders scene-linear, like Karma: Houdini's viewer applies the display transform.

To see the image Unreal's editor would show, turn on Unreal Tonemapper (unreal:tonemapper) above the tabs. UE then applies its film curve, bloom and colour grading. The beauty becomes display-linear: view it with an sRGB view that only encodes, not Raw or ACES.

Unreal Tonemapper, in Realtime:

Turn it off again for this tutorial's EXR, so the image stays scene-linear for compositing.

items.title: Render to disk with husk
items.text:
1. Save the scene, for example as cornell.hip.
  2. Add a USD Render ROP LOP after the hdUE Render Settings LOP.
  3. Set Render Delegate to Unreal Engine.
  4. Click Render to Disk.

husk writes the image to the Output Picture of the hdUE Render Settings LOP, $HIP/render/$HIPNAME.$OS.$F4.exr by default: a numbered EXR in the render folder next to cornell.hip.

You can also render the sample file directly from a terminal:

husk --renderer "Unreal Engine" -o cornell.exr "$env:HDUE\samples\cornell\cornell.usda"

On an RTX 4090, the Cornell box takes about 2.3 s per frame in the Path Tracer and about 50 ms in Realtime, after about 3 s of Unreal Engine startup per husk process (Gallery).

items.title: Final render settings
items.text:
• Render Mode: Path Tracer (Realtime (Lumen) for the fast version)
  • Path Tracer Samples: 512
  • Unreal Tonemapper: off
  • Camera: /cornell_box/camera
  • Resolution: 512 x 512

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Solaris viewport: the Unreal Engine tab, the Unreal menu and viewport speed.
  • Rendering with husk: frame ranges, farms and render products.
  • Render settings reference: every setting with its default.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
hdUE ships as one folder plus a Houdini package file, the way HtoA or Redshift install. You build the folder once on a machine with the Unreal Engine source, then copy it to each workstation or render node.

Unreal Engine licensees only

The package contains Unreal Engine Developer modules, which the Unreal Engine EULA calls Engine Tools. Section 6(d) allows sharing such a package only through Fab or a fork of Epic's UnrealEngine GitHub network: inside your studio, or with other Unreal Engine licensees. Never publish it as a public download. There is no prebuilt download for this reason: you build your own package.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
On each machine that renders:

Requirement Value Operating system Windows 10 or 11, x64 Houdini 22.0, the build the package was compiled against or a later 22.0 build GPU DirectX 12 with hardware ray tracing Runtime libraries Microsoft Visual C++ 2015-2022 x64 redistributable (Houdini installs it)

The workstations need no Unreal Engine, Visual Studio or OpenUSD.

On the machine that builds the package, you need the Unreal Engine 5.8.4 source and the toolchain listed in Building from source.

items.title: Building the package
items.text:
Run these from the root of the hdUE checkout, after a first build as described in Building from source:

.\scripts\Build-Backend.ps1 -Configuration Test # (1)!
.\scripts\Update-HoudiniRuntime.ps1 -Configuration Test -OutputConfig .local\runtime-release.json # (2)!
.\scripts\Package-Houdini.ps1 -RuntimeConfig .local\runtime-release.json -Zip -UnrealLicenseesOnly # (3)!
  1. Build-Backend.ps1 -Configuration Test builds Unreal Engine in Epic's Test configuration: Shipping's optimizations, with the console variables that hdUE's unreal:cvar:* settings need.
  2. Update-HoudiniRuntime.ps1 stages that build into a runtime profile.
  3. Package-Houdini.ps1 writes the package. -UnrealLicenseesOnly confirms the distribution terms above; the script refuses to run without it.

The script also refuses to package when:

  • the profile's backend is not the current Test build;
  • the checkout has uncommitted changes;
  • the Houdini delegate was built from another commit (run .\scripts\Build-Houdini.ps1 first).

The result is in out\package\:

File Contents hdUE-<version>-houdini<build>-win64\ The package folder, about 1.2 GB. For example hdUE-v0.2.0-houdini22.0.368-win64. hdUE-<version>-houdini<build>-win64.zip The same folder zipped, about 0.9 GB. hdUE-<version>-houdini<build>-win64-symbols.zip Debug symbols. Keep it with the release to read crash dumps; do not ship it.

<version> is the checkout's git describe. The delegate DLL's file properties (Details tab) show the same version and the Houdini build it was compiled for.

items.title: Installing on a workstation
items.text:
1. Unzip the package folder where it will stay. A shared, read-only network folder works: each user's logs and shader cache go to their own Houdini preferences folder.
  2. Close Houdini.
  3. Double-click Install.cmd in the package folder.
  4. Start Houdini.

Install.cmd writes one file, Documents\houdini22.0\packages\hdUE.json (or under HOUDINI_USER_PREF_DIR when you set it). Houdini, hython and husk all read it at startup. It sets the variables listed in Environment variables and adds the Solaris integration to HOUDINI_PATH.

If you move the folder, run Install.cmd again.

items.title: Studio-wide install
items.text:
Write the package file into a shared package folder instead of each user's Documents:

.\Install.ps1 -PackagesDirectory \\server\houdini\packages

Point every machine's HOUDINI_PACKAGE_DIR at that folder.

items.title: Checking that it works
items.text:
1. In a Solaris Scene Viewer, open the renderer menu. Unreal Engine is listed.
  2. Pick it. The first time in a session, Unreal Engine starts inside Houdini; the viewport shows the scene a few seconds later.

  3. In a terminal, run:

    husk --renderer "Unreal Engine" -o check.exr "$env:HDUE\samples\cornell\cornell.usda"

    husk writes check.exr, the Cornell box at 512 x 512.

Then follow Your first render.

items.title: Uninstalling
items.text:
1. Run Uninstall.cmd in the package folder. It deletes hdUE.json and nothing else.
  2. Delete the package folder.

For a studio install, pass the same folder: .\Uninstall.ps1 -PackagesDirectory \\server\houdini\packages.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Unreal Engine is missing from the renderer menu. Houdini did not load hdUE.json: it is missing, or this Houdini is older than the build the package was compiled for. Run Install.cmd again and restart Houdini. Check that your Houdini build is at least the one in the package name. Incomplete hdUE package: ... is missing. when you run Install.cmd. The folder was partly copied or unzipped. Unzip the whole package again. hdUE warning: hdUE was built against Houdini 22.0.<build> but runs in Houdini 22.0.<other build> SideFX guarantees binary compatibility only within one Houdini build. Nothing to do if renders work. If rendering crashes or misbehaves, build a package for this Houdini build. The viewport stays empty after you pick Unreal Engine. Unreal Engine failed to start. Open Unreal > Open Unreal Engine Logs and read the newest log.

items.title: Houdini
items.text:
hdUE adds Unreal Engine as a renderer to Houdini 22.0 Solaris. The viewport, husk, the USD Render ROP and Live Render all load the same renderer and read the same unreal:* render settings, so a farm renders what your viewport shows.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Houdini["fal:fa-house Houdini"]
        S("fal:fa-layers LOP network<br/>USD stage")
        V("fal:fa-monitor Solaris viewport")
        R("fal:fa-clapperboard USD Render ROP")
        H("fal:fa-square-terminal husk")
        L("fal:fa-radio Live Render LOP")
        C("fal:fa-image Copernicus")
    end
    E("fal:fa-file-image EXR files")
    S --> V
    S --> R --> H --> E
    S --> L --> C

    classDef host stroke-width:1px
    classDef hdue stroke-width:1px
    classDef unreal stroke-width:1px
    classDef output stroke-width:1px

    class Houdini,S,V,R,H,L,C host
    class E output

items.text:

    Picking Unreal Engine, the Unreal Engine tab, the Unreal menu, keeping the viewport fast.

    Solaris viewport

  • Rendering with husk

    Command lines, frame ranges, farms, render products, failures.

    Rendering with husk

  • Live Render and Copernicus

    Rendering into a Live Render LOP for compositing.

    Live Render and Copernicus

  • Substrate materials

    Building UE Substrate materials in a VOP network.

    Substrate materials

  • AOVs in Houdini

    Render vars, hdUE Standard Render Vars, Cryptomatte.

    AOVs in Houdini

  • COP and embedded textures

    op: images and textures embedded in assets.

    COP and embedded textures

items.title: The hdUE LOPs
items.text:
The package adds these LOPs to the TAB menu under hdUE:

LOP TAB menu Karma counterpart hdUE Render Settings hdUE > Rendering Karma Render Settings hdUE Standard Render Vars hdUE > Rendering Karma Standard Render Vars hdUE Render Products hdUE > Rendering Karma Render Products hdUE Height Fog, hdUE Sky Atmosphere, hdUE Volumetric Cloud, hdUE Local Fog Volume hdUE > Visual Effects hdUE Post Process Volume, hdUE Decal hdUE > Visual Effects hdUE Unreal Asset hdUE > Scene hdUE Substrate Material Builder hdUE (in /mat and Material Library LOPs) Karma Material Builder

The Visual Effects LOPs place Unreal Engine's scene components as USD prims, filed as UE's Place Actors panel files them. See Fog, Sky and clouds and Post-processing. The Unreal Asset LOP imports an asset from another UE project and places it: see Game effects.

items.title: Rendering with husk
items.text: husk is Houdini's command-line USD renderer. With hdUE installed, husk --renderer "Unreal Engine" renders a USD file with Unreal Engine, using the render settings saved in the file. The USD Render ROP runs husk the same way, so the viewport, the ROP and a farm render the same image.

items.title: Command lines
items.text:
Render frames 1 to 24 of a USD file:

husk --renderer "Unreal Engine" -f 1 -n 24 -o render.$F4.exr scene.usd
Option What it does --renderer "Unreal Engine" Renders with hdUE. -f 1 First frame. -n 24 Number of frames. -o render.$F4.exr Output image, overriding the render products' names. --settings /Render/rendersettings The render settings prim, when the file holds several. -V 3 Prints progress as it renders (see Progress). --tile-count 2 2 --tile-index 0 Renders one tile of a 2 x 2 grid.

Relative output paths resolve from the folder you run husk in, as with other renderers.

items.title: From Houdini
items.text:
1. Add a USD Render ROP LOP after your render settings, or a USD Render node in /out.
  2. Set Render Delegate to Unreal Engine.
  3. Turn on Render All Frames with a Single Process.
  4. Click Render to Disk.

Step 3 matters: each husk process starts Unreal Engine once. See Frame ranges.

A USD Render ROP after the render settings, its Render Delegate set to Unreal Engine.

items.title: Frame ranges and farms
items.text:
Unreal Engine starts once per husk process, and stays until the process exits. Between frames, husk sends only what changed. Render a frame range in one husk call, and give farm tasks chunks of frames, not one frame each.

On an RTX 4090, measured on scenes of this repository:

Scene Startup per process Per frame after the first Cornell box, 512 x 512, Realtime about 3 s about 50 ms Intel's Sponza, 2560 x 1440, Realtime, animated camera and sun about 30 s (UE and the scene's meshes) about 0.3 s, of which 0.2 s is husk writing the float EXR

Nanite builds are cached on disk across processes, so the second husk run of a scene skips most of its mesh building.

items.title: Realtime sequences
items.text:
In Realtime, husk renders a frame range the way Movie Render Queue renders a shot:

  1. The first frame renders Warmup Frames (unreal:warmupFrames, default 64) frames, so Lumen, anti-aliasing and eye adaptation settle.
  2. Each later frame draws once and keeps that temporal history.

A sudden change between frames, such as a light switched on, therefore catches up over the next few frames, as in Unreal Engine. Render each cut as its own husk call, or pass husk's --restart-delegate <n>, which restarts the renderer every n frames; each restart warms up again.

items.title: Farm setup
items.text: Each render node needs the hdUE package installed (Installation), a Houdini 22.0 build the package supports, and a DirectX 12 GPU with hardware ray tracing.

items.title: Render products and AOVs
items.text:
husk writes every render product of the render settings. Use hdUE's LOPs to author them:

  • hdUE Render Settings: Output Picture and one toggle per AOV on its Image Output tab.
  • hdUE Standard Render Vars: the beauty, depth, normals, lighting components, IDs and Cryptomatte, each with its precision.
  • hdUE Render Products: several output images, each with its render vars.

See AOVs for what each AOV holds and costs, and Alpha for the alpha channel.

husk also honours the render settings' data window (crops and overscan), the pixel aspect ratio and husk's tiling (--tile-count, --tile-index, --autotile): each render covers only its window (Cameras). A single render is at most 16384 pixels a side; render larger images in tiles.

items.title: Output format
items.text:
The EXR is husk's. Writing it costs more than the compression choice. Measured on the Cornell box at 2560 x 1440, per frame of a sequence:

Beauty format Compression Time per frame File size Float (color4f) ZIP 269 ms 9.4 MB Float none 257 ms Half (color4h) ZIP 195 ms 5.2 MB Half none 194 ms Half PIZ 249 ms

hdUE's part is about 70 ms of each; the rest is husk. For a cheaper beauty, set the beauty render var's dataType and driver:parameters:aov:format to color4h.

items.title: Progress and logs
items.text:
husk verbosity Prints -V 2 Each frame's start, and its render time at the end. -V 3 Progress while rendering: Path Tracer samples or Realtime warmup, Unreal Engine startup, scene upload, textures and mesh builds with the time left. -V 5 Also the scene statistics after each frame.

husk's output also shows every Unreal Engine warning and error, each warning once. For every line of Unreal Engine's log, set HDUE_UE_ARGS=-stdout. The full log is in %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\Saved\Logs (Environment variables).

items.title: Exit codes and failures
items.text:
husk exits with a non-zero code when a frame fails, so a farm manager marks the task as failed. That happens when:

  • Unreal Engine fails to render the frame;
  • none of the requested render vars is one hdUE renders;
  • a material the frame needs could not be prepared (Substrate materials).
Symptom Cause Fix An AOV is empty (its clear value), with a warning in husk's output. hdUE does not render that render var: a light path expression other than the beauty's, or a primvar. Use an AOV from the AOV table. Resolution ... is outside 1..16384, the largest texture this GPU's RHI renders The image is larger than Unreal Engine's largest render target. Render in tiles: --autotile --tile-count 2 2. hdUE warning: hdUE was built against Houdini ... The render node runs another Houdini 22.0 build than the package's. See Installation. Each frame takes several seconds longer than expected. One husk process per frame: Unreal Engine starts each time. Render frame ranges per process (see Frame ranges).

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text:
• Command lines are Karma's with --renderer "Unreal Engine"; the same USD file can hold both renderers' settings.
  • In Realtime, sequence frames reuse their history as Movie Render Queue does; Karma renders each frame independently.

items.title: Live Render and Copernicus
items.text: The Live Render LOP renders the stage in the background while you edit it, and sends the image to the Render Gallery. With hdUE, it renders with Unreal Engine; a File COP can then bring that image into Copernicus for compositing.

items.title: Rendering with Live Render
items.text:
1. Add a Live Render LOP after your render settings.
  2. Set Render Delegate to HdUnrealEngine.
  3. Set Render Settings to your render settings prim, or leave it empty to use the stage's default.
  4. Click Start Render.

The render reacts to upstream LOP edits, as in the viewport. Click Stop Render to end it.

One hdUE render per session

A Houdini session renders one hdUE image at a time. Before you start a Live Render with hdUE, switch the Scene Viewer to another renderer, and the other way round.

items.title: In Copernicus
items.text:
1. Add a File COP.
  2. Set Source to Live Render.
  3. Set Live Render LOP to your Live Render node.

The File COP can start and stop the render itself. See SideFX's Live rendering in Solaris.

What the tests check

hdUE's tests check that a Live Render converges with its AOVs. They do not check the image that reaches the File COP: check it in your scene.

items.title: Render settings
items.text: Live Render reads the same unreal:* settings as the viewport and husk. See Solaris viewport and the Render settings reference.

items.title: Substrate materials
items.text:
Substrate is Unreal Engine's material model: surfaces built from slabs, layered and mixed. In Houdini you build a Substrate material in a VOP network, the way you build a Karma material with the Karma Material Builder. hdUE then turns it into a native UE material.

Needs the Unreal Engine editor

A changed Substrate network is compiled by Unreal Engine's editor, which the hdUE package does not include. Preparing a material needs a machine with the UE editor and an hdUE source checkout (Building from source). On a machine with the package only, an unprepared Substrate material fails the husk frame. Prepared materials render everywhere.

items.title: Creating a material
items.text:
1. Add a Material Library LOP.
  2. Inside it, press Tab and choose hdUE > hdUE Substrate Material Builder. It starts with a Substrate Slab wired to the surface output.
  3. Dive into the builder and add hdUE Substrate nodes from the TAB menu (hdUE submenu), filed as UE's Material Editor palette files them: Substrate, Parameters, Constants, Math, Coordinates, Texture, Utility and Volume.
  4. On the Material Library LOP, assign the material to your geometry, as with any material.

You can also create the builder in /mat and point the Material Library's Material VOP at it.

The hdUE shelf has the same builder, plus:

  • Water Coating Example: a builder with a clear water slab layered over a MaterialX base, with coverage and roughness parameters.
  • Author Substrate USD: adds a Material Library LOP after the displayed LOP that authors the selected builder at /Looks/<builder name> and binds it to the current Scene Graph selection.

See Substrate Builder for every node and its inputs.

items.title: Editing
items.text:
You change What happens A value: colour, roughness, thickness, a parameter The viewport updates at once. A node type, a wire, a parameter name, a blending option hdUE prepares the material again in the background. Houdini's status bar shows the progress; the viewport keeps the last valid image until it is ready. A texture's file contents only Nothing: re-prepare the material by hand.

Background preparation is on by default: Prepare Edited Materials (unreal:substrateAutoPrepare, reference) on hdUE Render Settings > Rendering > Materials. husk reads the same setting and prepares the materials a frame needs before rendering it. A material is prepared once per runtime: later renders reuse it.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix The material stops updating after you disconnect a node. A required surface or output is disconnected. Reconnect it; preparation resumes. A husk frame fails with a message about an unprepared material. Prepare Edited Materials is off, or the machine has no UE editor. Turn the setting on, or prepare the material on a machine with the editor first. Preparation failed and stays failed after you fixed the cause. A failed network is retried only when its nodes or wires change. Change a node or a wire in the network.

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text:
• The builder is made the way SideFX makes the Karma Material Builder: an editable VOP subnet with a material flag.
  • Its nodes are UE's Substrate expressions, not Karma shaders: Karma does not render these materials.

items.title: Solaris viewport
items.text:
The Solaris Scene Viewer renders with Unreal Engine once you pick Unreal Engine in its renderer menu. Unreal Engine runs inside Houdini on its own thread, so a slow frame never blocks Houdini's UI.

The Scene Viewer rendering with Unreal Engine (Path Tracer, 512 samples), the hdUE Render Settings LOP's parameters, and the network: a Sublayer, hdUE's settings, the render settings and a USD Render ROP.

items.title: Picking Unreal Engine
items.text:
1. Display a LOP network in a Scene Viewer.
  2. In the viewer's renderer menu, pick Unreal Engine, or choose Unreal > Use Unreal Engine in the Viewport.

The first time in a session, Unreal Engine starts inside Houdini; the image appears a few seconds later. It then stays loaded until Houdini exits, so switching back to Unreal Engine is immediate.

One Houdini session renders one hdUE image at a time: one viewport, or one Live Render.

Selection works as with Karma: click a prim in the viewport to select it, and Solaris outlines it. The outline appears once the view is still.

items.title: Render settings
items.text: hdUE reads its settings from unreal:* attributes on the stage's render settings prim. You set them in three places.

items.title: hdUE Render Settings LOP
items.text:
hdUE Render Settings (TAB menu > hdUE > Rendering) is the counterpart of Karma Render Settings: one LOP with the camera, resolution, Output Picture and every hdUE setting. Unreal > Create hdUE Render Settings adds one after the displayed LOP.

From top to bottom it shows:

  1. Show: Essential | Advanced. Essential shows what Unreal's editor shows by default; Advanced adds the settings UE keeps behind its Advanced expanders. Settings hidden by Essential still render. When a hidden setting differs from its default, a notice names it, with a Show in Advanced button.
  2. The camera and output: Output Picture ($HIP/render/$HIPNAME.$OS.$F4.exr by default), camera, resolution (up to 16384 pixels a side; render larger images in husk tiles) and pixel aspect ratio.
  3. The main settings: Render Mode, Path Tracer Samples or Warmup Frames, Unreal Tonemapper and Exposure Compensation. See Above the tabs.
  4. One tab per Unreal Engine category, in the order of UE's Details panel:
Tab Holds Rendering Anti-aliasing and screen percentage, Path Tracing, View Mode, Geometry, Materials Lens Bloom, Exposure, Chromatic Aberration, Dirt Mask, Camera, Local Exposure, Lens Flares, Image Effects, Depth of Field Color Grading Temperature, Global, Shadows, Midtones, Highlights, Misc, Film, Film Grain Lighting Global Illumination (Lumen), Reflections, Shadows, Dome and Viewer Lights Fog Exponential Height Fog and Volumetric Fog Sky Sky Atmosphere and Volumetric Cloud Rendering Features Post-process materials, MegaLights, Ambient Occlusion, Motion Blur, Translucency Image Output Render products and one toggle per AOV Engine Quality Scalability, Nanite, Ray Tracing

Settings that one render mode ignores are hidden in that mode. For example, Lumen and Shadows are hidden with the Path Tracer, and Path Tracer Samples is hidden in Realtime. A hidden setting keeps its value.

items.title: Render Settings LOP
items.text: Houdini's own Render Settings LOP gets the same settings on an Unreal Engine tab. As with Karma's properties, each setting starts unauthored: set its control menu to author it.

items.title: Viewport Display Options
items.text:
The viewport's Display Options get an Unreal Engine tab with the settings you change while working: Render Mode, Warmup Frames, Path Tracer Samples, Debug View, Motion Blur, Lumen, Light Unlit Scenes, Viewer Light Intensity, Subdivision Level, Unreal Tonemapper and the Engine Quality group (scalability, anti-aliasing, DLSS, screen percentage, hardware ray tracing, Virtual Shadow Maps).

Console variables apply to the whole session

Settings named unreal:cvar:* are Unreal Engine console variables. They apply to the whole Houdini process, so they change every hdUE render in the session until you change them back.

items.title: Light and geometry settings
items.text: Light LOPs get an Unreal Engine tab for the per-light unreal:* properties (Light properties). Render Geometry Settings LOPs get one for per-prim settings: a cooked native UE asset, hair, and wet surfaces.

items.title: The Unreal menu
items.text:
The package adds an Unreal menu to Houdini's main menu bar, before Windows.

Entry What it does Use Unreal Engine in the Viewport Picks Unreal Engine in the Scene Viewer, as the renderer menu does. Render Mode > Realtime / Path Traced Sets Render Mode on the first Render Settings or hdUE Render Settings LOP above the displayed LOP. If there is none, adds an hdUE Render Settings LOP after the displayed LOP. Create hdUE Render Settings Adds an hdUE Render Settings LOP after the displayed LOP and displays it. It takes the camera, render mode and samples from the stage's existing render settings, if any. Caches > Show Cache Sizes Lists each hdUE disk cache with its size, file count and folder. Caches > cache > Open Folder Opens that cache's folder. Caches > cache > Clear... Asks, then deletes the cache's contents. Caches > Clear All hdUE Caches... Asks, then deletes the contents of every cache. Open Unreal Engine Logs Opens the folder of Unreal Engine's logs. Documentation Opens this guide's Houdini pages in your browser.

items.title: Caches
items.text:
hdUE keeps four disk caches so a scene's second load is faster. They are per user and live on the system drive, outside synced folders. Each process removes entries unused for a week. Clear a cache to reclaim its space at once, or after a problem you suspect comes from stale cache data.

The texture caches grow with the textures of the scenes you open, and can take tens of GB: on one development workstation, the texture cache held 12 GB and the virtual texture cache 35 GB. The Nanite cache stayed under 1 GB there.

Cache Folder Holds Texture %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\TextureCache Block-compressed textures Virtual texture HDUE_VIRTUAL_TEXTURE_CACHE, else %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\VirtualTextureCache UDIM virtual textures Nanite %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\Saved\NaniteCache, or Saved\NaniteCache under HDUE_USER_DIR Nanite mesh builds OCIO texture %TEMP%\hdue_ocio Textures converted to the OCIO working space

To move the virtual texture cache, the largest, to another drive, set HDUE_VIRTUAL_TEXTURE_CACHE; HDUE_USER_DIR moves the Nanite cache and Unreal Engine's logs. The texture cache stays in %LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE.

Clearing is refused once Unreal Engine has started in the session, because it reads the cache files while it runs. Restart Houdini and clear before you pick Unreal Engine. Files another process holds open (husk, another Houdini) are kept and listed.

items.title: Viewport speed
items.text:
While you tumble, scrub or play, the viewport renders a cheaper image, then refines it once the view is still. In the Path Tracer, it renders 8 samples per pixel while you move:

Symptom Cause Fix The Realtime image is soft while you move, then sharpens. Lower Resolution While Moving renders at Moving Screen Percentage (50%) until 250 ms after the last change. Raise Moving Screen Percentage, or turn off Lower Resolution While Moving. The Path Tracer is noisy while you move. It renders 8 samples per pixel until the view is still. None needed: it refines to Path Tracer Samples once you stop. The selection outline appears late or flickers. The outline needs two extra ID renders per view, which run only once the view is still. Set int unreal:viewportIdAovs = 0 on the render settings to skip them. Selection then works from the Scene Graph Tree only, without an outline. Realtime is slow at every frame. Lumen, shadows and reflections run at Epic quality. Lower the Engine Quality groups (Shadows, Global Illumination, Reflections) from Epic (3) to High (2), or lower Screen Percentage. The viewport renders far more pixels than it shows. Display Options > Render > Image Resolution is set to the render settings' resolution. Use the viewport's size while you work. Materials first show flat colours, then their textures. Textures decode and compress in the background. The progress line under the viewport counts the files done and the time left. Wait; the second load of a scene reads them from the texture cache. Meshes appear a moment after the scene loads. Meshes upload as standard meshes first, then are swapped for Nanite meshes in the background. Wait; Nanite builds are cached on disk, so the next session skips most of them. The viewport shows a black or stale image while husk renders fine. Frames pass from Unreal Engine to Houdini's OpenGL viewport on the GPU, which needs the GPU driver's shared-memory extensions. Set HDUE_GPU_FRAMES=0 before starting Houdini to copy frames through the CPU instead.

To measure where a frame's time goes, set HDUE_TRACE_TIMING=1 and HDUE_TRACE_FILE=<path> before starting Houdini (Environment variables).

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text:
• The renderer settings live on the same render settings prim as Karma's, so a scene can carry both.
  • hdUE's LOPs mirror Karma's: hdUE Render Settings, hdUE Standard Render Vars and hdUE Render Products work like their Karma counterparts.

items.title: COP and embedded textures
items.text: A texture input can read a Copernicus (COP) image live from the Houdini session, or an image embedded in a digital asset, as Karma does. Edit the COP network and the material updates in the viewport.

items.title: Using it in Solaris
items.text:
1. Build the image in a Copernicus network.
  2. In a USD UV Texture or MaterialX Image node, set File to the COP node's path with the op: prefix: op:/obj/geo1/copnet1/OUT.
  3. To read another output of the node, add its index: op:/obj/geo1/copnet1/OUT[1]. The default is output 0.

The same paths work in light textures (a dome light's or a rect light's Texture).

  • Edits to the COP network, including time-dependent ones, reach the viewport within a tick. The Path Tracer restarts its accumulation when an image changes.
  • An image the session has not exported yet renders untextured for a moment.
  • Images are exported as 32-bit float with no colour conversion. Colour inputs then go through the OCIO scene_linear space as any EXR does (Colour management); inputs with Source Color Space raw stay as they are.
  • Legacy COP colour planes need integer frames.

items.title: Embedded images
items.text: opdef: paths, images stored inside a digital asset, render as files: Houdini extracts each image once, without changing the asset or the USD.

items.title: Rendering with husk
items.text: husk has no Houdini session to cook op: paths in. Save the stage with a USD Render ROP or USD ROP: as for Karma, they write each op: image next to the USD (a tiled, mip-mapped EXR) and rewrite its path, so husk renders ordinary files.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Symptom Cause Fix husk renders a COP texture untextured, with a warning naming the op: path The stage was saved without the ROP, so it still holds op: paths Render through the USD Render ROP, or write the COP image to a file and point the texture at it A COP texture shows in the viewport but a UDIM collection from COPs does not COP UDIM collections are not supported Write the tiles to files with a <UDIM> pattern

COP images cannot replace textures inside a cooked UE asset.

items.title: MaterialX surfaces
items.text:
hdUE renders MaterialX Standard Surface and OpenPBR Surface materials, the surfaces of Karma's and Houdini's MaterialX builders. It translates them at render time onto UE's own Standard Surface material functions, the ones UE's Interchange uses to import MaterialX, so edits show immediately, with no compile.

The figures on this page use the shader ball (samples/docs/lookdev.usda) in Realtime with a Standard Surface shader. Below: Preview Surface, then Standard Surface with transmission, subsurface and sheen.

items.title: Using it in Solaris
items.text:
1. In a Material Library LOP, create a Karma Material Builder (or a MaterialX subnet) holding a MaterialX Standard Surface or MaterialX OpenPBR Surface.
  2. Wire textures with MaterialX Image nodes, as below.
  3. Assign the material. A material with both a MaterialX output and a Preview Surface output renders from its MaterialX graph.

If a graph uses a node outside the list below, UE's MaterialX importer prepares it in the background (automatic import). Until it is ready, that input renders at its constant value, with a warning naming the node.

items.title: Base
items.text:
Standard Surface OpenPBR Default In UE Base base × Base Color base_color base_weight × base_color 1 × (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) Base colour Metalness metalness base_metalness 0 Metalness, as Preview Surface Metallic

diffuse_roughness is not translated.

items.title: Specular
items.text:
Standard Surface OpenPBR Default In UE Specular specular × Specular Color specular_color 1 × (1, 1, 1) Specular tint, on materials with coat, sheen or subsurface Specular Roughness specular_roughness specular_roughness 0.2 Roughness Specular IOR specular_IOR specular_ior 1.5 Dielectric reflectance, as Preview Surface IOR

Anisotropy is not translated.

items.title: Transmission
items.text:
Transmission USD attribute transmission (OpenPBR transmission_weight) Default 0

Above 0, the surface refracts: hdUE uses UE's translucent Standard Surface material, as Interchange imports a transmissive MaterialX surface, in Realtime and in the Path Tracer. transmission_color tints the light passing through and transmission_depth (scene units) is the distance at which it reaches that colour. See Opacity and glass for the settings, figures and recipes.

items.title: Subsurface
items.text:
Subsurface USD attribute subsurface (OpenPBR subsurface_weight) Default 0

Light enters the surface, scatters and exits nearby: skin, wax, marble, milk. hdUE renders it as Substrate subsurface scattering.
