Intensity (unreal:postProcess:BloomIntensity) · Default 0.675 · Range 0 to 8 · reference

Glow around bright pixels. 0 turns bloom off. Threshold (default -1) makes every pixel bloom in proportion to its brightness, as a real lens does. Preferred Method switches to Convolution, an FFT bloom shaped by a Kernel image, which costs more.

items.title: Chromatic Aberration
items.text:
Intensity (unreal:postProcess:SceneFringeIntensity) · Default 0 · Range 0 to 5 · reference

Colour fringes towards the frame's corners, in percent. Start Offset (0 to 1) moves where the fringes begin, from the centre outwards.

items.title: Lens Flares
items.text:
Intensity (unreal:postProcess:LensFlareIntensity) · Default 1 · Range 0 to 16 · reference

Image-based flares from pixels brighter than Threshold (default 8). Lower the threshold to get flares from dimmer highlights; each step down blurs more of the image and costs more. BokehShape takes an image for the flare's shape.

items.title: Dirt Mask
items.text:
Dirt Mask Intensity (unreal:postProcess:BloomDirtMaskIntensity) · Default 0 · Range 0 to 8 · reference

Lens dirt lit by bloom. Set Dirt Mask Texture to an image of the dirt, then raise the intensity.

items.title: Vignette
items.text:
Vignette Intensity (unreal:postProcess:VignetteIntensity) · Default 0.4 · Range 0 to 1 · reference

Darkens the frame's corners. 0 turns it off. The Advanced parameters set its Vignette Type (cosine-fourth law, oval or a texture), centre, size, softness and colour.

items.title: Sharpen
items.text:
Sharpen (unreal:postProcess:Sharpen) · Default 0 · Range 0 to 10 · reference

Sharpens the image during tonemapping.

items.title: Color Grading
items.text: All grading works on the scene-linear image before the film curve, as in UE. Saturation, Contrast, Gamma, Gain and Offset are four numbers: red, green, blue and an overall multiplier. Each exists for the whole image (Global) and for Shadows, Midtones and Highlights.

items.title: Temperature
items.text:
Temp (unreal:postProcess:WhiteTemp) · Default 6500 K · Range 1500 to 15000 · reference

The white balance of a virtual camera: the light temperature that renders white. Below the scene's light temperature the image turns blue, above it yellow. Temperature Type set to Color Temperature inverts this. Tint (-1 to 1) shifts along the magenta-green axis.

items.title: Saturation
items.text:
Saturation (unreal:postProcess:ColorSaturation) · Default (1, 1, 1, 1) · Range 0 to 2 · reference

0 is black and white, 1 leaves the image unchanged, above 1 strengthens colours. The captions give the fourth (overall) value.

items.title: Contrast, Gamma, Gain, Offset
items.text: Parameter Attribute Default What it does Contrast unreal:postProcess:ColorContrast (1, 1, 1, 1) Spreads values away from middle grey Gamma unreal:postProcess:ColorGamma (1, 1, 1, 1) Brightens or darkens the midtones Gain unreal:postProcess:ColorGain (1, 1, 1, 1) Multiplies the image Offset unreal:postProcess:ColorOffset (0, 0, 0, 0) Adds to the image: lifts the blacks

items.title: Film
items.text:
Method (unreal:postProcess:TonemappingMethod) · Default Filmic · reference

The film curve. Slope (0.88), Toe (0.55), Shoulder (0.26), Black clip (0) and White clip (0.04) shape it. Tone Curve Amount (1) fades it out: set it and Expand Gamut to 0 to remove the curve completely.

items.title: Film Grain
items.text:
Film Grain Intensity (unreal:postProcess:FilmGrainIntensity) · Default 0 · Range 0 to 1 · reference

Grain over the image. Film Grain Intensity Shadows, Midtones and Highlights weight it per range; Film Grain Scale sets its size.

items.title: Color Grading LUT
items.text:
Color Grading LUT (unreal:postProcess:ColorGradingLUT) · Default empty · reference

A lookup table in UE's format: a 256 x 16 image of 16 slices, red across a slice, green down, blue across the slices. Color Grading LUT Intensity (0 to 1) blends it in.

items.title: Texture parameters
items.text:
Parameters that take a texture (Color Grading LUT, Dirt Mask Texture, Film Grain Texture, Vignette Texture, Lens Flare BokehShape, the convolution bloom Kernel, Exposure Metering Mask, Ambient Cubemap) accept either:

  • an image file: EXR, HDR, PNG, JPG, TIF, TGA or BMP. A relative path resolves against the USD layer that authors it. 8-bit files are read as sRGB, float files as linear. Editing the file updates the render.
  • a cooked texture in the runtime project: /Game/... or /Engine/....

A file that cannot be read is skipped with a warning in the UE log (%LOCALAPPDATA%\hdUE\Saved\Logs).

items.title: Post-process materials
items.text:
Post-Process Materials (unreal:postProcessMaterials) · Default empty · reference

Cooked UE post-process materials, by path, separated by spaces. They are added to the beauty as UE blendables. Materials whose Blendable Location is Before Tonemapping also work with the tonemapper off.

items.title: Post-process volumes
items.text:
A post-process volume applies its settings only while the camera is inside it or within its blend radius, as UE's Post Process Volume does.

  1. Add hdUE Post Process Volume (TAB menu > hdUE > Visual Effects). In Create mode it shows a guide box: the volume fills the cube from -1 to 1 of its transform.
  2. Set Priority, Blend Radius and Blend Weight, or turn on Infinite Extent (Unbound) to cover the whole scene.
  3. Turn on the settings it should change: each starts at Do Nothing, like UE's override checkboxes.
Parameter Attribute Default What it does Priority unreal:postProcessVolume:Priority 0 The higher priority wins where volumes overlap Blend Radius unreal:postProcessVolume:BlendRadius 100 Distance around the box over which the volume fades in, in UE centimetres Blend Weight unreal:postProcessVolume:BlendWeight 1 0 no effect, 1 full effect Enabled unreal:postProcessVolume:bEnabled On Infinite Extent (Unbound) unreal:postProcessVolume:bUnbound Off Covers the whole world

The render settings apply after every volume, as a camera's settings do in UE: a setting authored on hdUE Render Settings wins over all volumes. Volumes need the tonemapper on for exposure and grading, like the render settings. See UnrealPostProcessVolume.

items.title: Decals
items.text:
A decal projects a material onto the surfaces inside a box, as UE's Decal Actor does.

  1. Add hdUE Decal (TAB menu > hdUE > Visual Effects). In Create mode it shows a guide box: the decal fills the cube from -1 to 1 of its transform and projects down its local down axis.
  2. Bind a decal material: a Substrate Builder decal material, or set Decal Material (unreal:decal:DecalMaterial) to a cooked Deferred Decal material path.
  3. Optionally set Decal Color (unreal:decal:DecalColor, default white), which the material reads through UE's Decal Color node. Sort Order (0): higher values draw on top of overlapping decals. Fade Screen Size (0.01) fades the decal when it is small on screen.

A decal with no material draws nothing. A material that is not a decal material is skipped with a warning. See UnrealDecal.

items.title: How to match UE's editor look
items.text:
1. Unreal Tonemapper: on.
  2. Lens > Exposure > Metering Mode: Auto Exposure Histogram.
  3. Exposure Compensation: 1 (UE's project default).
  4. View with Un-tone-mapped.

Bloom 0.675, vignette 0.4 and the Filmic curve are already UE's defaults. The camera's exposure still adds to the compensation: set it to 0 for a scene exposed for Karma. On Sponza, this lands about 0.6 stops above the camera's authored exposure.

items.title: How to get a filmic grade for a still
items.text:
1. Unreal Tonemapper: on; Metering Mode: Manual.
  2. Exposure Compensation: adjust until middle grey reads right, typically 0 to 2.
  3. Temp: 7500 (warmer than neutral). Saturation: (1, 1, 1, 1.15).
  4. Bloom Intensity: 1.5. Vignette Intensity: 0.5.
  5. Chromatic Aberration Intensity: 4. Film Grain Intensity: 0.35.

samples/cornell/variants/post_processing.usda shows these effects on the Cornell box.

items.title: How to grade but keep a linear EXR
items.text:
1. Unreal Tonemapper: on; Disable Tone Curve: on.
  2. Set the grade (Temp, Saturation, Contrast, ...). Leave grain and vignette off if comp will add them.

The EXR is scene-linear, graded, in your config's scene_linear space.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Bloom, grading or vignette have no effect The Unreal Tonemapper is off Turn on Unreal Tonemapper. Exposure Compensation has no effect The Unreal Tonemapper is off Turn it on, or use the camera's Exposure, which works either way. Image much darker with the tonemapper on The film curve compresses values below middle grey (0.03 becomes 0.011) Raise Exposure Compensation. Image too dark and crushed Viewed with Raw Use Un-tone-mapped. Exposure flickers between frames Auto exposure Set Metering Mode to Manual. A post-process setting is ignored, with a warning in the UE log The property name or value is unknown Check the spelling against the reference. Viewport shadows black, husk EXR fine Houdini 22.0.368's viewport OCIO display shows linear values below about 0.004 as black Judge dark images in the EXR.

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text:
• Every parameter is UE's FPostProcessSettings property, with UE's default, except exposure: hdUE renders with manual exposure and Exposure Compensation 0, where UE defaults to Auto Exposure Histogram with compensation 1. This keeps middle grey where the linear image has it and makes frames repeatable.
  • With the tonemapper off, hdUE's beauty is scene-linear like Karma's. Karma has no equivalent of UE's tonemapper; grade Karma renders in comp or in Copernicus.
  • For the same stage and settings, Houdini's viewport and husk give the same beauty: on the Cornell box with the tonemapper on, within 3% in mean and 1.5/255 in sRGB at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles.

items.title: Render settings
items.text:
Render settings choose how Unreal Engine renders your stage: the render mode, its sample counts and UE's post-processing. They are unreal:* attributes on the stage's UsdRenderSettings prim, so Houdini's viewport and husk render with the same settings.

The Cornell box in both render modes.

items.title: Realtime or Path Tracer
items.text:
hdUE has two render modes, the two renderers of UE itself.

Realtime (Lumen) Path Tracer What it is UE's deferred renderer, with Lumen global illumination and reflections, MegaLights and Virtual Shadow Maps UE's reference path tracer, which accumulates samples per pixel Cornell box, 512 x 512 48 ms per frame 2.34 s per frame (512 samples) Intel Sponza, 960 x 540 84 ms per frame 6.64 s per frame (256 samples) Noise none; Lumen settles over its warmup frames falls with the sample count, then the denoiser removes the rest Use it for look development, layout, animation previews, final frames that must render in milliseconds reference images, glossy and refractive detail, final frames where accuracy matters more than time

Times are per frame in husk on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, from the gallery. A Realtime time is a sequence frame after the first frame's warmup.

Lumen approximates glossy reflections of small, bright lights. On SideFX's Veach planks, the Path Tracer resolves each light on each plank.

Lumen also approximates bounce light. In the Bistro, lit by its lamps, compare Realtime without global illumination, Realtime with Lumen and the Path Tracer.

items.title: Using render settings in Solaris
items.text:
HoudiniUSD
  1. Add an hdUE Render Settings LOP (TAB menu > hdUE > Rendering), or use any Render Settings LOP: with hdUE installed, it gets an Unreal Engine tab.
  2. Set the essential settings above the tabs: Render Mode, Path Tracer Samples or Warmup Frames, Unreal Tonemapper and Exposure Compensation.
  3. Find the rest in the tabs, laid out as UE's editor lays them out: Rendering, Lens, Color Grading, Lighting, Fog, Sky, Rendering Features, Engine Quality.
  4. On hdUE Render Settings, click Show: Advanced to see the settings UE's editor keeps behind its Advanced expanders. A notice under the strip names the changed settings that Essential hides.

Each control authors nothing until you change it, as on Karma's render settings. Settings that one render mode ignores are hidden in that mode.

hdUE Render Settings: Show: Essential | Advanced, the output and camera, the main Unreal Engine settings, then one tab per UE category.

The viewport's Display Options have an Unreal Engine tab with the settings you change while working: render mode, samples, warmup, debug view, motion blur, Lumen, subdivision, the tonemapper and the main scalability groups. The Unreal menu in Houdini's main menu bar switches Render Mode too.

Outside Houdini, author the attributes on the render settings prim:

def RenderSettings "Settings"
{
    token unreal:renderMode = "pathtraced" # (1)!
    int unreal:samplesPerPixel = 256 # (2)!
    bool unreal:tonemapper = 1 # (3)!
    float unreal:postProcess:AutoExposureBias = 1 # (4)!
}
  1. Render Mode: the Path Tracer.
  2. Path Tracer Samples.
  3. Unreal Tonemapper on.
  4. Exposure Compensation, in stops.

Three families cover all 371 settings:

  • hdUE's own settings: unreal:renderMode, unreal:samplesPerPixel, unreal:motionBlur, ...
  • unreal:postProcess:<Property>: any property of UE's post-process settings (FPostProcessSettings), with UE's name.
  • unreal:cvar:<console variable>: a UE console variable, with : in place of . because USD attribute names cannot hold dots. int unreal:cvar:r:Shadow:Virtual:Enable = 0 sets r.Shadow.Virtual.Enable 0. See Engine quality.

items.title: Render Mode
items.text:
Render Mode (unreal:renderMode), default Realtime (Lumen).

Realtime renders with UE's deferred renderer and Lumen. Path Tracer renders with UE's path tracer. Path Tracer frames take 40 to 80 times longer than Realtime frames in the gallery scenes above.

items.title: Path Tracer Samples
items.text:
Path Tracer Samples (unreal:samplesPerPixel), default 2048, range 1 to 65536. Path Tracer only.

Samples per pixel. Render time grows in proportion to the samples; noise falls with their square root, so 4 times the samples halves the noise. With motion blur, the samples are divided between the motion sub-frames.

The Cornell box with the denoiser off.

Tip

With the denoiser on, you need far fewer samples: the gallery's Sponza renders with 256. Raise the samples when the denoised image smears fine texture or contact shadows.

items.title: Warmup Frames
items.text:
Warmup Frames (unreal:warmupFrames), default 64, range 1 to 256. Realtime only.

The frames UE renders before a frame counts as finished, so that Lumen's lighting and UE's temporal effects settle. The default is the warmup of Movie Render Queue's default configuration. In husk, only the first frame of a sequence warms up; each later frame continues from the previous one with one draw, as in Movie Render Queue.

Lumen gathers its bounce light over frames: too few warmup frames leave it dark and blotchy.

items.title: Unreal Tonemapper
items.text:
Unreal Tonemapper (unreal:tonemapper), default off.

Runs UE's tonemapper with its film curve, bloom, colour grading, vignette and film grain. On, the beauty is UE's display image: view it in Houdini with an sRGB view that only encodes (Un-tone-mapped), not Raw. Off, the beauty stays scene-linear for your OCIO view. See Post-processing and Colour management.

Disable Tone Curve (unreal:disableToneCurve, default off) keeps the tonemapper's effects without the film curve, as Movie Render Queue's setting of the same name. hdUE turns it on when your OCIO config's default view is ACES or AgX.

items.title: Exposure Compensation
items.text:
Exposure Compensation (unreal:postProcess:AutoExposureBias), default 0, range -15 to 15, in stops. Needs the Unreal Tonemapper.

Each step doubles or halves the image's brightness before the tone curve. The USD camera's exposure adds to it. Exposure stays manual, so frames are repeatable; UE's auto exposure is under Lens > Exposure (Metering Mode).

items.title: Viewport and husk
items.text:
The same settings render differently while you work in the viewport, so that it stays responsive:

  • While you tumble, scrub or play, the Path Tracer renders at most 8 samples. It renders your full sample count once the view is still.
  • While the camera or scene changes, Realtime renders at 50% screen percentage and upscales (Lower Resolution While Moving). Full resolution returns 250 ms after the last change.
  • The selection highlight's ID passes render only once the view is still.

husk and the USD Render ROP render with an offline profile, like Movie Render Queue's Game Overrides:

  • every scalability group at Cinematic (the viewport uses Epic);
  • every texture fully streamed in before the frame renders;
  • no GPU timeout, so long Path Tracer frames are not reset by Windows.

Settings you author win over both profiles.

items.title: All settings
items.text: The render settings reference lists every setting with its attribute, default, range and UE's tooltip, tab by tab: Rendering, Lens, Color Grading, Lighting, Fog, Sky, Rendering Features, Engine Quality.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Realtime bounce light is dark or blotchy in husk too few warmup frames Raise Warmup Frames to the default 64. Path Tracer image is noisy in the viewport while you move the viewport caps samples at 8 while moving Stop moving; the full sample count renders. Path Tracer image keeps its noise in the final frame the denoiser is off, or too few samples Turn Denoiser on, or raise Path Tracer Samples. See Denoising. Exposure Compensation does nothing the Unreal Tonemapper is off Turn Unreal Tonemapper on, or use the camera's exposure. Colours look wrong with the tonemapper on the viewer applies its own display transform, or none (Raw) Set the viewer to Un-tone-mapped sRGB. A setting is missing from the LOP it applies to the other render mode, or it is Advanced Switch Render Mode, or click Show: Advanced.

items.title: Unreal Engine and Karma
items.text: The defaults are UE's: Realtime with Lumen, 64 warmup frames as Movie Render Queue, and the Path Tracer's own settings from UE's post-process settings. Karma has no Realtime mode. Karma's Diffuse Limit N matches the Path Tracer's Max. Bounces N + 1.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text:
Each tutorial produces one result from a scene in samples/, with exact values at every step. Start with Your first render if you have not rendered with hdUE yet.

  • Lighting an interior

    Light the Bistro at night: practical lamps, a key light, haze and dust, the lens and a grade.

    Lighting an interior

  • Lumen or the Path Tracer

    When to use each render mode, where Lumen differs on four scenes, and how to close the gap.

    Lumen or the Path Tracer

  • Removing noise

    Find the cause of grain, fireflies, blotches, trails or grainy shadows, and the one setting that fixes it.

    Removing noise

  • Exposure and tone

    Scene-linear or UE's tonemapper, exposure, UE's editor look, and EXRs for comp.

    Exposure and tone

  • Depth of field and motion blur

    Focus and aperture on a row of toys, shutter and motion samples on a moving ball.

    Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: Depth of field and motion blur
items.text:
A row of toys focused on the fourth one, at f/2.

You will focus a camera on a row of toys and set its aperture, then blur a moving ball with the camera's shutter. Both effects come from the USD camera, so the same camera settings also drive Karma. It takes about 20 minutes.
path: Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: The starting scenes
items.text:
• Depth of field: $HDUE/samples/docs/row.usda. Seven rubber toys stand 1.2 m apart in front of the camera /scene/camera, which is 2.4 m from the first toy. The fourth toy is 6 m away. The camera has Focus Distance 6 and F-Stop 0, which means no depth of field.

  • Motion blur: $HDUE/samples/cornell/variants/motion_blur.usda. A blue ball crosses the Cornell box during frame 1; the camera's shutter opens a quarter frame before the frame and closes a quarter frame after.

  • In /stage, add a Sublayer LOP with File $HDUE/samples/docs/row.usda and set its display flag.

  • Render with Unreal Engine through camera, and choose Unreal > Create hdUE Render Settings. Keep Render Mode at Realtime (Lumen).
path: Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: Aperture
items.text:
The aperture sets how quickly objects blur away from the focus distance. A lower f-stop is a wider aperture and a shallower depth of field.

The row at F-Stop 0, 8 and 2, focused at 6 m.

  1. Add a Camera LOP. Set Action to Edit and Primitive Path to /scene/camera.
  2. Set F-Stop (fStop) to 2. 0 turns depth of field off. hdUE passes the f-stop, focus distance and focal length to UE's physical camera.
path: Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: Focus
items.text:
The row at F-Stop 2, focused at 2.4 m (the first toy), 6 m (the fourth) and 9.6 m (the last).

  1. Set Focus Distance (focusDistance) to the distance of the subject, in scene units: 6 for the fourth toy. Measure it from the camera, not from the origin.
path: Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: Realtime and the Path Tracer
items.text:
Realtime uses UE's post-process depth of field, an approximation that clamps very large blur. The Path Tracer traces the lens itself (Reference Depth Of Field, unreal:postProcess:PathTracingEnableReferenceDOF, which hdUE turns on when the camera has depth of field).

The row at f/2 in Realtime and in the Path Tracer.

  1. For extreme blur, macro shots or bokeh that must be exact, render with the Path Tracer.
  2. In Realtime, Number of diaphragm blades (unreal:postProcess:DepthOfFieldBladeCount, default 5, Lens tab) shapes the bokeh.

To turn depth of field off for a render without editing the camera, author disableDepthOfField = 1 on the render settings prim. See Cameras.
path: Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: Shutter
items.text:
Motion blur needs two things: a camera whose Shutter Open is before its Shutter Close, and something that moves during that interval. Motion Blur (unreal:motionBlur) is on by default.

  1. Replace the Sublayer's File with $HDUE/samples/cornell/variants/motion_blur.usda and look through camera.
  2. On the hdUE Render Settings LOP, set Render Mode to Realtime (Lumen).
  3. Add a Camera LOP in Edit mode for /cornell_box/camera. Set Shutter Open to -0.25 and Shutter Close to 0.25. The shutter is in frames, relative to the frame: this is a half-frame shutter centred on the frame, a 180° shutter.

The ball with a quarter-frame, half-frame and full-frame shutter.

A longer shutter makes longer streaks; the ball covers more distance while the shutter is open.
path: Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: Motion samples
items.text:
hdUE renders the frame several times across the shutter and averages them: Motion Samples (unreal:motionSamples, default 16, Rendering Features tab) sets how many. In Realtime the warmup frames are divided between them; in the Path Tracer, the samples. The total render time stays about the same.

The ball with 1, 4 and 16 Motion Samples.

  1. Keep Motion Samples at 16. With too few, a fast object shows as separate copies instead of a streak. Raise it for very fast motion or long shutters.

What moves: transforms of meshes, curves, points and their parents, camera transforms, deforming meshes (time-sampled points or velocities), and instancer and point velocities. See Motion blur for the full list. Deforming meshes are uploaded again for each motion sample, which costs time on dense meshes.

The ball in Realtime and in the Path Tracer.

To render without motion blur, turn Motion Blur off, or author disableMotionBlur = 1 on the render settings prim.
path: Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: Final render settings
items.text:
• Camera: F-Stop 2, Focus Distance the subject's distance; Shutter Open -0.25, Shutter Close 0.25.
  • Render Mode: Realtime (Lumen); the Path Tracer for exact bokeh.
  • Motion Blur: on; Motion Samples: 16.
path: Depth of field and motion blur

items.title: Exposure and tone
items.text:
The Bistro with UE's tonemapper off (the scene-linear image, sRGB-encoded) and on.

You will choose between a scene-linear image for compositing and UE's tone-mapped image, set exposure, match the look of UE's editor, and deliver EXRs for comp. It takes about 20 minutes.

items.title: The starting scene
items.text:
Use the Bistro, $HDUE/samples/docs/bistro.usda (see Lighting an interior for the download): a night interior with a wide range of brightness, from the glowing lamp shades to the dark corners.

  1. In /stage, add a Sublayer LOP with File $HDUE/samples/docs/bistro.usda and set its display flag.
  2. Render with Unreal Engine through camera, and choose Unreal > Create hdUE Render Settings.

Set Unreal Tonemapper off on the LOP to start from the scene-linear image.

items.title: Scene-linear or tone-mapped
items.text:
Unreal Tonemapper (unreal:tonemapper, default off) decides what the beauty holds.

  • Off: the beauty is scene-linear HDR, like Karma's. Houdini's OCIO view does the display, and values above 1 are kept for comp.

  • On: UE applies its film curve, bloom, colour grading, vignette and grain, as its editor viewport and Movie Render Queue do. The beauty is UE's tone-mapped image, display-linear Rec.709.

  • Set Unreal Tonemapper to on.

  • Keep the viewport on Houdini's default view (sRGB display, Un-tone-mapped). That view only encodes for the monitor, so it shows what UE shows. Raw shows the image too dark; an ACES or AgX view would tone map it a second time.

UE's film curve keeps middle grey (0.18) where it is. It darkens shadows (0.03 becomes 0.011) and rolls highlights off toward white (1 becomes 0.72, 4 becomes 0.94). A scene lit with most of its content far below middle grey therefore looks darker with the tonemapper; raise the exposure rather than the lights.

Bloom, colour grading, vignette, grain, chromatic aberration and lens flares only exist inside the tonemapper: with it off, they do nothing. See Post-processing.

items.title: Exposure compensation
items.text:
Exposure Compensation (unreal:postProcess:AutoExposureBias, default 0, above the tabs) shifts the exposure in stops: +1 doubles the brightness, -1 halves it.

The Bistro at -1, 0, +1 and +2 (the scene itself authors +1).

  1. Raise Exposure Compensation one stop at a time until the shaded corners read, then check that the lamp shades keep their detail. The film curve rolls highlights off, so a stop more brightens the mid-tones more than the lamp shades.

It applies with the tonemapper on. With the tonemapper off, change exposure on the camera instead (below) or in comp.

items.title: Camera exposure
items.text:
The camera's Exposure (exposure, in stops, on the Camera LOP) works with either setting:

  • tonemapper off: it scales the beauty, as in Karma; AOVs are left unscaled;

  • tonemapper on: it is added to Exposure Compensation.

  • On a Camera LOP in Edit mode for /scene/camera, set Exposure to 1. With the tonemapper on, this is the same image as Exposure Compensation 1. Keep exposure on the camera when the shot also renders in Karma, so both renderers read the same value.

items.title: Matching UE's editor
items.text:
hdUE starts from UE's settings with one exception: exposure is manual (Metering Mode Manual, compensation 0), so frames are deterministic and middle grey stays 0.18. A new UE project uses auto exposure: Auto Exposure Histogram, UE's default metering mode (Auto Exposure), with a project exposure bias of 1 (r.DefaultFeature.AutoExposure.Bias, UE source SceneView.cpp).

Manual exposure (hdUE's default), then UE's default auto exposure.

To see the image UE's editor viewport shows for the same scene:

  1. Turn Unreal Tonemapper on.
  2. On the Lens tab, set Metering Mode (unreal:postProcess:AutoExposureMethod) to Auto Exposure Histogram.
  3. Set Exposure Compensation to 1.

Auto exposure measures every frame on its own, so a sequence's exposure can shift from frame to frame, and two renders of the same frame can differ by several percent. In the viewport it reaches its target on every frame unless you set Speed Up or Speed Down (unreal:postProcess:AutoExposureSpeedUp, AutoExposureSpeedDown); husk always uses the target. Use manual exposure for final frames. See Lens reference.

items.title: Delivering for comp
items.text:
Comp wants scene-linear EXRs. You have two ways to get them.

Tonemapper off. The beauty is scene-linear in the OCIO config's scene_linear role, ACEScg in an ACES pipeline. Grade and tone map in comp. See Colour management.

Tonemapper on, tone curve off. When the shot needs UE's bloom or grading in the render, turn on Disable Tone Curve (unreal:disableToneCurve, default off). This is Movie Render Queue's Disable Tone Curve: grading, bloom, vignette and grain still apply, without the film curve, so the beauty stays scene-linear.

The Bistro with the tonemapper on, with Disable Tone Curve off and on.

  1. Keep Unreal Tonemapper on and set Disable Tone Curve to on.
  2. View the result through your OCIO view (ACES, AgX or Un-tone-mapped), as you would a Karma render.

When the OCIO config's default view is a display transform of its own (ACES, AgX), hdUE turns the tone curve off by itself, as UE does when OpenColorIO does the display. Post-processing applies to the beauty only: AOVs stay raw for comp.

items.title: Final render settings
items.text:
• For comp: Unreal Tonemapper off, exposure on the camera.
  • For comp with UE's bloom or grading: Unreal Tonemapper on, Disable Tone Curve on.
  • For UE's look in the frame: Unreal Tonemapper on, Metering Mode Manual, Exposure Compensation set by eye.

items.title: Lighting an interior
items.text:
The shot at the end of this tutorial: the Bistro at night, a warm spot on the near table, haze around the lamps, dust in the beam, the bar falling out of focus.

You will start from the restaurant lit by its own lamps, then give the image a subject with a key light, add atmosphere with volumetric fog and dust, shape it with the lens, and finish with a grade. Each stage changes one thing. It takes about 45 minutes.

items.title: The starting scene
items.text:
The scene is the interior of Amazon Lumberyard Bistro (NVIDIA ORCA, CC BY 4.0), converted to USD with MaterialX standard surfaces by scripts/convert_bistro.py. The download is not part of hdUE: samples/bistro/README.md lists the steps (download, then one hython command).

samples/docs/bistro.usda sublayers the converted scene and adds the shot: its lights, haze, dust, camera settings and grade. This tutorial switches them on one at a time.

  1. In /stage, add a Sublayer LOP with File $HDUE/samples/docs/bistro.usda, and set its display flag.
  2. Pick Unreal Engine in the viewport's renderer menu, and the Bistro's Camera in its camera menu.
  3. Choose Unreal > Create hdUE Render Settings. Keep Render Mode on Realtime (Lumen) and check that Unreal Tonemapper is on.

items.title: Practical lights
items.text:
A real room is lit by its lamps: the photographer's "practicals". The conversion puts a 2700 K sphere light of 5 cm inside each of the twelve lamp shades, next to their glowing emissive glass.

  • Exposure 10 on each lamp: a 5 cm bulb is a small source, so it needs a high exposure to light a room.
  • Exposure Compensation (unreal:postProcess:AutoExposureBias) +1: a night interior, exposed one stop over UE's starting point.
  • The shades are milk glass: they must not block their bulb. Each light's shadow link excludes the shades, so they cast no shadows (UE has no per-light shadow exclusion; a mesh outside every light's shadow link casts none).

Lit only by its lamps, the room is even and flat: nothing tells the eye where to look.

items.title: A key light
items.text:
Give the image a subject. A warm spot from the ceiling onto the near table makes the table the brightest place in the frame; the lamps become the fill and the back of the room falls off.

  1. Add a Light LOP: Type Sphere, Radius 0.04, Exposure 12, Color Temperature 3000 K.
  2. Turn on Spot Light (ShapingAPI): Cone Angle 22, Cone Softness 0.5. A soft edge reads as a real fixture, not a stage spot.
  3. Place it 2.6 m above the near table, pointing down.

A warmer key (3000 K) than the room's lamps (2700 K) would be too orange; matching them keeps the light motivated: it looks like one more lamp in the restaurant.

items.title: Haze and dust
items.text:
Air in a busy room is never clean. A thin volumetric fog lets the lights draw their shape in the air, and a few motes of dust catch the key.

  1. On the Fog tab, turn on Exponential Height Fog with Fog Density 0.05 and Fog Height Falloff 0.02 (nearly even at every height in a room).
  2. Turn on Volumetric Fog: lights scatter into the fog and the shades cast shadows in it.
  3. On the lights, raise Volumetric Scattering Intensity (unreal:light:VolumetricScatteringIntensity) to 2: the lamps glow in the air without lighting the room more.
  4. For dust, add a Points prim inside the key's cone: 700 points, 1.5 to 3 mm wide, with a pale MaterialX standard surface. Dust shows only where light hits it, so place it in the beam, not the whole room.

Fog density

Keep the fog thin. At Fog Density 0.1 the room turns milky and the shadows lose their depth; 0.03 to 0.05 reads as air.

items.title: The lens
items.text:
A photographer at this table would open the aperture: the near glass sharp, the bar soft behind it. The camera's fStop and focusDistance drive UE's depth of field (USD lens values are in tenths of a scene unit; focusDistance is in scene units).

  1. On the camera, set F-Stop to 2.8.
  2. Set Focus Distance to the near wine glass: 1.37 m here. Measure it in the viewport with the camera's Focus Distance handle, or from the glass's bounds.

items.title: The grade
items.text:
A final touch of film: a little grain and a white balance a touch warmer than daylight.

  • Film Grain Intensity (unreal:postProcess:FilmGrainIntensity) 0.12: enough to break up the smooth gradients of the haze, not enough to notice.
  • White Temp (unreal:postProcess:WhiteTemp) 6000: UE's white balance, set slightly below the 6500 K default, warms the whole image.

items.title: Lumen and the Path Tracer
items.text: The same shot in both render modes (the figure at the top of this page). Both show the haze, the key's pool and the depth of field; the Path Tracer's bounce light and glass are the reference, Lumen renders the frame in a fraction of the time.

items.title: Final render settings
items.text:
• Render Mode: Realtime (Lumen), or Path Tracer for the reference
  • Unreal Tonemapper: on, Exposure Compensation +1
  • Lamps: 2700 K, Exposure 10, shades outside every shadow link
  • Key: sphere spot, 3000 K, Exposure 12, cone 22°, softness 0.5
  • Exponential Height Fog: on, Fog Density 0.05, Fog Height Falloff 0.02, Volumetric Fog on
  • Camera: F-Stop 2.8, Focus Distance 1.37
  • Film Grain Intensity 0.12, White Temp 6000

items.title: Lumen or the Path Tracer
items.text:
hdUE renders in one of UE's two modes. Realtime (Lumen) is UE's deferred renderer with Lumen global illumination and reflections, the renderer of a game or a Movie Render Queue shot. Path Tracer is UE's reference renderer. This page shows both on four scenes, names where Lumen differs and how to close the gap.

The Cornell box in Realtime and in the Path Tracer.

Switch with Render Mode (unreal:renderMode) on the hdUE Render Settings LOP, or Unreal > Render Mode. Every scene below is in samples/ and renders unchanged in both modes.

items.title: Choosing
items.text:
Realtime (Lumen) Path Tracer A frame 64 warmup frames for a still; one draw per frame after the first in a husk sequence Path Tracer Samples (default 2048), denoised Noise Converges over frames; can leave blotches in indirect light Grain that falls with samples; the denoiser removes the rest Bounces Lumen's multi-bounce approximation Up to Max. Bounces (default 32) Reflections One bounce; traced up to roughness 0.4 Every bounce, every roughness Use it for Look development, animation, final frames Reference images, glass and mirrors, stills where render time allows

On the gallery's Global illumination Cornell box at 512 x 512 on an RTX 4090, a Lumen sequence frame takes 48 ms and the Path Tracer 2.34 s at 512 samples (Gallery). Times are measured on the figures below.

Realtime is not a preview mode: UE renders final frames with it, and so can you. Use the Path Tracer to check what Lumen approximates, or when a shot depends on what Lumen does not do.

items.title: Four scenes side by side
items.text:
The Bistro (samples/docs/bistro.usda), lit by its lamps: most of the room is lit by bounced light.

The Veach planks (samples/docs/veach.usda): four sphere lights of increasing size over four planks of increasing roughness.

The shader ball studio (samples/docs/lookdev.usda).

Surfaces lit directly by a light match closely between the two modes. The differences are in bounced light and reflections.

items.title: What Lumen approximates
items.text:
Each item comes from UE's Lumen documentation (Lumen Global Illumination and Reflections, Lumen Technical Details).

Symptom in Realtime Cause Fix Blotches in mirror reflections indoors Lumen lights its own scene at low quality for reflections Raise Lumen Scene Lighting Quality, or set Ray Lighting Mode to Hit Lighting for Reflections Small objects black in mirror reflections Lumen culls small objects from its scene Raise Lumen Scene Detail Rough metal looks flat or blurry Above Max Roughness To Trace (0.4), Lumen traces no dedicated reflection rays Raise Max Roughness To Trace No reflections inside reflections Max Reflection Bounces is 1 Raise it; UE supports more than 1 only with hardware ray tracing and hit lighting (Ray Lighting Mode) A small emissive object lights the room unevenly, or noisily Small, bright emissive areas are hard for the final gather, and small objects are culled Use a light for a small source; keep emissive surfaces large A smooth base under a clear coat reflects as rough Lumen traces one reflection ray per pixel; only the top layer can be smooth Use the Path Tracer for smooth clear-coated surfaces Indirect light from a linked light reaches every object UE's lighting channels restrict direct light only The Path Tracer honours light links exactly (Lights)

items.title: Glossy reflections
items.text:
The ball as polished metal (roughness 0.1): Realtime with the default Ray Lighting Mode, with Hit Lighting for Reflections, and the Path Tracer.

  1. On the Lighting tab, set Ray Lighting Mode (unreal:postProcess:LumenRayLightingMode) to Hit Lighting for Reflections. Reflection rays are lit where they hit instead of from Lumen's surface cache. UE recommends it for the highest-quality mirror reflections; it costs GPU time.
  2. For many smooth surfaces, also raise Quality under Lumen Reflections (unreal:postProcess:LumenReflectionQuality) from 1 to 2. It reduces noise in reflections.

The ball as rough metal (roughness 0.55), with Max Roughness To Trace at 0.4 and 1.

  1. For rough metals, raise Max Roughness To Trace (unreal:postProcess:LumenMaxRoughnessToTraceReflections) above the material's roughness. UE's tooltip: higher values improve reflection quality but greatly increase GPU cost.

items.title: Bounced light
items.text:
1. Set Ray Lighting Mode to Hit Lighting. Lumen's diffuse rays are then lit at their hit point too. See Lighting an interior for an interior in both modes.
  2. If indirect light stays blotchy, raise Final Gather Quality to 2. See Removing noise.
  3. Do not raise Diffuse Color Boost or Indirect Lighting Intensity to match the Path Tracer. UE's tooltip says values of Diffuse Color Boost above 1 are not physically correct; they brighten bounced light for art direction, not accuracy.

items.title: The Path Tracer's own limits
items.text:
• Grain needs samples; see Removing noise.
  • Ambient Cubemap lights the scene in Realtime only.
  • Fireflies are clamped by Max Path Intensity (24), which removes some energy from bright indirect paths.

items.title: Final render settings
items.text:
• Animation and look development: Render Mode Realtime (Lumen), Warmup Frames 64, Ray Lighting Mode Hit Lighting for Reflections when the shot has mirrors.
  • Reference stills: Render Mode Path Tracer, Path Tracer Samples 2048, Denoiser on.
  • All settings: Render settings and the Lighting reference.

items.title: Removing noise
items.text:
Noise has a different cause in each render mode. The Path Tracer converges by adding samples; Realtime converges over frames, and its noise comes from Lumen, shadows and the temporal anti-aliasing. Find your symptom below, then change the one setting that fixes it.

The Path Tracer at 16 samples without the denoiser, at 512 samples, and at 16 samples with the denoiser.

flowchart TD
    A("fal:fa-scan-eye Noisy or flickering image") --> B{Render Mode?}
    B -->|Path Tracer| C{What kind of noise?}
    C -->|Fine grain everywhere| D("fal:fa-sliders-horizontal Path Tracer Samples, Denoiser")
    C -->|Isolated bright pixels| E("fal:fa-flame Max Path Intensity")
    C -->|Grainy soft shadows| D
    B -->|Realtime| F{What kind of noise?}
    F -->|Blotches in indirect light| G("fal:fa-timer Warmup Frames, Final Gather Quality")
    F -->|Blotches in reflections| H("fal:fa-sparkles Lumen Scene Lighting Quality, Reflection Quality")
    F -->|Trails behind moving objects| I("fal:fa-waves Anti-Aliasing Method, Lighting Update Speed")
    F -->|Grainy soft shadows| J("fal:fa-sun-moon Soft Shadow Rays, MegaLights per light")

    classDef host stroke-width:1px
    classDef hdue stroke-width:1px
    classDef unreal stroke-width:1px
    classDef output stroke-width:1px

    class A output
    class B,C,F hdue
    class D,E,G,H,I,J unreal

The scenes: the Cornell box for the Path Tracer, the Bistro (samples/docs/bistro.usda) for Lumen, the chrome ball and box (samples/docs/lights.usda) for shadows. All settings are on the hdUE Render Settings LOP.

items.title: Path Tracer: grain everywhere
items.text:
Cause. Too few samples per pixel. Each sample is one random light path; noise falls as the square root of the sample count, so 4 times the samples halves the noise.

  1. Leave Denoiser (unreal:postProcess:PathTracingEnableDenoiser) on, its default. It runs UE's NNE Denoiser (Open Image Denoise's network) on the last sample. See Denoising.
  2. Raise Path Tracer Samples (unreal:samplesPerPixel, default 2048) until the denoised image stops changing. The denoiser removes grain but also fine detail, so give it enough samples to keep texture and contact shadows. Render time grows in proportion to the samples.

The denoiser runs on the beauty only: AOVs stay noisy. In the viewport, the image stays noisy while it refines and is denoised once the last sample is in.

items.title: Path Tracer: fireflies
items.text:
Cause. Rare paths that find a bright light through a glossy bounce. Each one is a single very bright pixel that more samples average away only slowly.

Glossy Cornell box at 64 samples, denoiser off, with Max Path Intensity at 1000, 24 and 4.

  1. Keep Max Path Intensity (unreal:postProcess:PathTracingMaxPathIntensity) at 24, its default. It clamps the intensity of indirect samples. UE's documentation says the default clamps fireflies aggressively and rarely needs changing (Path Tracer).
  2. If fireflies remain, lower it to 4–10. Lower values clamp harder and lose some energy: bright reflections of bright surfaces darken.
  3. Keep Approximate Caustics (unreal:cvar:r:PathTracing:ApproximateCaustics) on, its default. It approximates caustic paths through smooth glass and metal, which reduces their speckles.

The clamp is relative to the exposure, so you do not need to change it with Exposure Compensation.

items.title: Realtime: blotches in indirect light
items.text:
Cause. Lumen has not settled, or its final gather traces too few rays for the scene. Blotches show on surfaces lit only by bounced light: ceilings, the shaded side of a room.

First check that the frame had time to settle. The Bistro with 1, 8 and 64 Warmup Frames.

  1. Keep Warmup Frames (unreal:warmupFrames) at 64, its default. These are the frames UE renders before a still counts as finished. In a husk sequence, only the first frame warms up; later frames continue from the previous one, as Movie Render Queue does.
  2. If blotches remain, raise Final Gather Quality (unreal:postProcess:LumenFinalGatherQuality, Lighting tab) from 1 to 2. It scales the rays Lumen's final gather traces. UE's tooltip: larger values reduce noise but greatly increase GPU cost.

The Bistro with Final Gather Quality at 0.25, 1 and 2.

See Lighting reference for the other Lumen settings.

items.title: Realtime: blotches in reflections
items.text:
Cause. Mirror-like reflections show Lumen's own simplified scene, which it lights at low quality. UE's documentation names this "splotchy artifacts in mirror reflections" (Lumen Technical Details).

  1. Raise Lumen Scene Lighting Quality (unreal:postProcess:LumenSceneLightingQuality) from 1 to 2.
  2. Raise Quality under Lumen Reflections (unreal:postProcess:LumenReflectionQuality) from 1 to 2. It reduces noise in reflections, at a GPU cost.
  3. For the cleanest mirrors, set Ray Lighting Mode (unreal:postProcess:LumenRayLightingMode) to Hit Lighting for Reflections. Reflection rays are then lit where they hit instead of read from the surface cache. See Lumen or the Path Tracer.

items.title: Realtime: trails behind moving objects
items.text:
Cause. Realtime accumulates over frames. Two parts of it can lag behind motion: the temporal anti-aliasing, which blends each frame with the previous ones, and Lumen, which caches its lighting between frames. This shows in sequences, not in a still.

  1. Keep Anti-Aliasing Method (unreal:cvar:r:AntiAliasingMethod, Rendering tab) at TSR, its default. UE's documentation says TSR ghosts less against detailed backgrounds than TAA (Anti-Aliasing and Upscaling).
  2. If trails remain on edges, set it to FXAA. FXAA works on one frame only, so it cannot ghost; edges alias more.
  3. If the lighting lags behind a moving light or object, raise Final Gather Lighting Update Speed (unreal:postProcess:LumenFinalGatherLightingUpdateSpeed) and Lumen Scene Lighting Update Speed (unreal:postProcess:LumenSceneLightingUpdateSpeed) from 1 to 2. Lighting changes then propagate faster, at a GPU cost and, for the final gather, more noise.

No figure here: a still render cannot show motion. Render a short sequence with husk to check.

items.title: Grainy soft shadows
items.text:
Cause. Soft shadows are sampled. In Realtime, local lights (rect, sphere, disk, spot) go through MegaLights, which samples lights stochastically and denoises the result; the distant light uses Virtual Shadow Maps, which trace a few rays per pixel through the shadow map. In the Path Tracer, shadows converge with the samples.

A distant light with a 5° angle, with 1 and 8 Directional Soft Shadow Rays (Realtime).

  1. For a distant light, keep Directional Soft Shadow Rays (unreal:cvar:r:Shadow:Virtual:SMRT:RayCountDirectional) at 8, its default, or raise it to 16. UE's documentation: fewer rays show noise in the penumbra (Virtual Shadow Maps).
  2. For local lights, MegaLights already takes 4 samples per pixel, UE's maximum (r.MegaLights.NumSamplesPerPixel supports 1, 2 and 4). Keep lights out of geometry and their influence tight instead. UE's documentation: every light that can reach a pixel shares a fixed sample budget, so hidden or overlapping lights add noise (MegaLights).
  3. If one local light's shadow stays grainy, turn MegaLights off for that light (unreal:megaLights = 0 on the light's Unreal Engine tab) and raise Local Soft Shadow Rays (unreal:cvar:r:Shadow:Virtual:SMRT:RayCountLocal) from 8 to 16. The light then uses UE's deferred lighting and Virtual Shadow Maps. See Lights.

The same scene in the Path Tracer at 16 and 256 samples, denoiser off.

  1. In the Path Tracer, raise Path Tracer Samples, as for grain.

items.title: Final render settings
items.text:
• Path Tracer: Denoiser on, Path Tracer Samples high enough that the denoised image is stable, Max Path Intensity 24.
  • Realtime: Warmup Frames 64, Final Gather Quality 1 (2 for noisy interiors), Anti-Aliasing Method TSR.
  • See Render settings for where each setting sits on the LOP.
